subtopic: RESPECTING SPEECH IN HOUSE ON SEPTEMBER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege. In this morning's Ottawa Citizen there is a headline which reads: " Score speeches by three M.P.'s on Ukrainians." The article then goes on to say:
Protesting "slanders and falsehoods" which, it claimed, are being disseminated through speeches by Walter Tucker, F. Zaplitny and A. Hlynka in the House of Commons, the Canadian Ukrainian Association has passed a resolution which states that the views expressed by these men are not those of the majority of Canadian Ukrainian people.
The article continues:
The association points out in the resolution that a body with headquarters in Winnipeg, the Canadian Ukrainian committee, is collects ing money to be used to aid "these nazi collaborationists and traitors to settle in Canada."
It goes on to say:
In the opinion of the association, the three members of parliament mentioned in the resolution, "actually speak on behalf of fascist and semi-fascist committees among the Ukrainian Canadians who have had previous connections with the nazi in Germany."
This refers to a speech which I made in this house on September 26, 1945, in reference to that subject. I have uttered no slanders and falsehoods. I merely asked that our troops have nothing to do with the forcible repatriation, into Soviet hands, of displaced Ukrainians whose only offence was that they had worked for and favoured a free Ukraine and who feared their fate if they fell into Soviet hands. I pointed out that no one knew for certain what was happening behind the iron curtain that divides Europe to-day and that if this policy were maintained we should not forcibly repatriate these people to what they claimed might be a terrible and undeserved fate.
The Canadian Ukrainian committee is headed by a distinguished Canadian clergyman. Its members are all loyal and distinguished Canadians. It supported, and the bulk of Ukrainians supported, our war effort, not only after Russia was attacked in 1941 but in the dark days of 1940, when those who followed the communist line were attacking the war as an imperialist war and doing their best to hinder our war effort. -
When I speak on behalf of this committee, representing as it does the vast bulk of Canadians of Ukrainian origin in Canada, I do not speak "on behalf of fascist and semifascist committees among Ukrainian Canadians who have had previous connections with the nazis in Germany." I deny this categorically. I say from long experience that the members of this committee are loyal and true Canadians. They have proved their loyalty. If they have sympathy with their kith and kin in Europe and seek to assist them in their misery, that does not make them pro-nazi or fascist.
Ever since I have spoken on behalf of these people I have been the victim of a slanderous smear campaign. The object is clear. It is to intimidate all public men from saying anything distasteful to the communists, no matter how true or justified it may be. I call on all responsible newspapers to study the situation and not lend themselves to these tactics in any way. I would say in conclusion it is an attempt subtly to undermine freedom of speech in Canada. It will not succeed in this free country.

There are powers under the Export Credits Insurance Act to make a loan or loans to the United Kingdom, but the financial limits of the government's powers are such that we do not propose to avail ourselves of the powers in that act to make a loan to the United Kingdom. We are not asking for enough money to give us the scope that we shall require. As I said yesterday, we have not discussed in any real sense a loan from Canada to the United Kingdom, the terms of the loan, the size of the loan or anything of the kind. We shall undoubtedly be discussing those terms before very long.
The only powers that we have to advance money on behalf of the United Kingdom to producers in Canada are the powers contained in section 3 of the War Appropriation Act, and we are making advances under section 3 of the War Appropriation Act at the present time. It will be understood that we owe the United Kingdom money on various accounts, and they owe us money on various accounts. These many and complicated matters are being examined and studied, but in the meantime I do not anticipate that we shall be embarrassed by the lack of any statutory power other than section 3 of the War Appropriation Act to make loans to the United Kingdom.

As the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario says, that is a matter that is more important than our dealings with any other country in the world, with the possible exception of the United States, our dealings with them being on a different basis entirely-the basis of -each one paying for what he buys and neither lending to the other, and so on.
It would be premature for me to say anything definite about what we intend or expect to do or can do with the United Kingdom. I agree with what the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario says; in fact, from what I recollect of what he says, I agree with it all. It is of tremendous importance that we should make satisfactory arrangements with the United Kingdom. It is of tremendous importance that we should keep trade flowing both ways with them. I do not intend to deal with that, except in passing, under this bill, which is designed to authorize loans to countries other than those in the sterling area. I indicated the possibility that some parts of the sterling area might avail themselves of the privileges of this bill, and in that connection I mentioned India, but I have nothing definite in mind.
Yesterday I said-and this touches upon the point raised by the member for Muskoka-Ontario-.that in our dealings with France we had stipulated for most favoured nation treatment, and that it was a term of the agreement. I find that the matter is referred to only in correspondence between the two countries, in a letter which I wrote to the representatives of the government of France as follows:
At this time, when Canada will be assisting France to increase substantially its imports from Canada for purposes of reconstruction, and when the Canadian government hopes to see an increase in exports from France to Canada, it seems to me appropriate to suggest that Canada and France might agree to extend to one another most favoured nation treatment in commercial policy. Such action would, I think, impress upon the people both of France and of Canada our intention to develop future trade between the two countries on a mutually advantageous basis.
I went on to say that I understood the Department of External Affairs would welcome an opportunity of discussing the possibility of such action with representatives of that government at an early convenient day. The relevant passage in the reply is as follows:
As regards your suggestion concerning the most favoured nation clause, this is a question which in due course will be discussed between [DOT]the representatives of our countries, _ but in conformity with the general principles included in the lend-lease master agreement, which is well known to you, and that France has signed,
I can now assure you that-the French government will collaborate with the Canadian government in concerted action to elminate all forms of discriminatory treatment in international commerce and to the reduction of tariffs and other trade barriers.
It is true that in these loan agreements we have not tied up these countries with regard to tariff treatment or similar treatment on Canadian exports into those countries, nor do I think it would be practicable to do so. The subject matter of these loan agreements is certain goods which will be ordered for the next two or three years, and of course [DOT] we need have no worry about these goods because they are buying them and taking them into their own country. So that the question of tariff treatment of these goods is not one of indifference to us, though it need not give us any worry, inasmuch as they are borrowing money to buy the goods.
To get a long-term agreement covering other goods during a subsequent period would be a very difficult task. It would involve long commercial negotiations, and the view we have taken is that such commercial negotiations should rest on their own feet. Our policy is to seek and try to obtain reciprocal reductions in trade barriers. The concessions that we would make would be tariff reductions, and the concessions we would seek would be tariff reductions in consideration of our reductions in tariff, without attempting the almost impossible task now of trying to tie up with these loans trade negotiations involving tariff treatment on a wide range of products coming into this country as well as going into those countries.
It may be that some principle should be kid down. In fact, principles were laid down in our mutual aid agreements with these other countries, but apart from general principles I do not think it would be practicable to incorporate in these loan agreements trade agreements covering goods other than the goods they intend to buy with these moneys.

I perhaps gave the minister a slight misunderstanding of what was in my mind. I should be loath to see us tie up with individual agreements, because, if I understand tariff matters rightly, every time you enter into a bilateral agreement with some country it raises difficulties in relation to the broad question of multilateral trade, which seems do me, frankly, the only solution for this country. I wish to reiterate a point I made a few minutes ago. I have been disturbed to find that apparently we have regarded ourselves as nothing more than interested spectators of

what has been going on at Washington. To me, we are so vitally concerned in this that I have never been able to feel that we were merely interested spectators.
I inferred from what the minister said that we had nobody actually sitting in at the Washington conference. I had thought that we had some economic observers, and I hoped that they were more than observers because I have always felt that we Canadians ought to be able to do more to bring Britain and the United States together than anybody else. We have talked a lot on that and I think with considerable justification. We have talked a lot about our influence in the world. I think we should have more influence on what is going on in Washington now. We should let it be known. If other hon. members feel as deeply concerned about what is going on in Washington as I do, I think that the house should go on record in the matter. It may be that what we say here would not fall entirely on deaf ears. We played a considerable part in the war; Britain has acknowledged that.
I think the time has come for us not to ask a quid pro quo but to try to play a very considerable part in connection with these trade negotiations which are going on. I want to make my position clear. We must have multilateral trade so that world trade will move, let us say, as freely as it did in the first decade of this century. I am not talking about free trade; that raises all kinds of difficulties. I am talking about a reasonable degree of freedom. Without it the prospect for this country is very bleak. I think we had better be specific about it. I hear people chant about full employment in a kind of incantation; they think that by repeating it we are going to get it. Well, many of the people who talk so glibly about full employment do not seem to understand the full implication of it.
I understand that yesterday someone said:
1 Why do not we take the money that it is proposed to use for these advances and use it :or social services?" The reason we are making these advances is to build up foreign trade so as to give us an income which will enable us to have social services. I hope I have not got the cart before the horse. Let us be frank about this. Let us not make fools of ourselves. Let us look at it in a realistic way and not forget the influence which I hope this country has. I suggest to the committee that there ought to be a debate on this matter in the house. If my views are the views of the members of the house then I think it is desirable that the people of Britain should know

it and know it in time, because they are not going to disregard what the people of Canada think.
I believe, and I say it again, with somewhat tiresome iteration, that multilateral trade is essential to this country. If we do not get multilateral trade we face economic reorganization. I was talking to a very competent economic friend of mine yesterday. He told me he had been discussing these matters with a man whom you might describe as an apostle of the new economic thinking. My friend asked the man to be specific and I will also be specific. Suppose we increase the consumption in this country by as much as we possibly can by internal arrangements; how much of the present wheat production will be consumed in Canada? The utmost that we can expect to consume in this country would be about twenty-five per cent of our production. If I am wrong in that, hon. gentlemen to my left will correct me. Am I wrong? If I am right, then where is the remainder of the wheat to go? If we are to have a tied-up regional world wherfe are we to export if we are not in the sterling bloc, into which incidentally we do not fit. Let anyone in the house tell me where. I want to use moderate language. If there is a bloc and all that it entails it is a serious thing for this country. I think we should omit nothing to prevent this. I do not think that a day or two devoted to this talk in parliament would be wasted. If other hon. members present have the views I hold, and to which I have been giving expression, their voice would be heard in Britain, and the views we hold would be known.

All right; then I should like to hear the right view. If Canada should be sitting in on this conference, then there is no reason in the world why she should not sit in on the conference between the United Kingdom and China, the United Kingdom and Brazil, the United Kingdom and the Argentine or the United Kingdom and any other country. I have no objection to this country having observers at the conference if we are asked so to do, but I am satisfied that it would not be the proper thing for Canada to assert that we should sit in at the conference.
The hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario said he had heard someone ask this question: "Why could we not expend for social services in Canada the moneys we are now expending to promote trade with other countries?" Perhaps that version of what he heard arose out of what I said in the house yesterday. Let me first of all assure the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario that I gave my wholehearted support to the export credits insurance bill and supported it, I think, on reasonable grounds. When he spoke a moment ago he said it was likely that we would be giving this money away. He then qualified that by saying that there was a possibility of our giving it away. If we are giving it away, if it is a matter of chance, is there any reason why we cannot give the same amount of money in social services to the people of Canada who need it? There is not. In the past as we looked across from Canada to some other country we have had the hope-I do not know whether we have got over it or not-that we could sell our goods there. We always looked
on those countries as a place where we could sell something. There are very fine people in China, we said, and we wondered if we could sell them something. There were very fine people in Brazil, and we wondered if we could sell them something. We always thought of them in terms of what we could sell them. That day has passed. We still have to think of them in terms of what we can sell them, but we have to think of them also in terms of what we can exchange with them in order that we may build up their economy, and by building up their economy we are assuring our prosperity and theirs. If it is not done on that basis it will not be done at all. That is what we must be concerned with from now on. As a matter of fact the old system of capitalist trade was a system which destroyed itself.
When we come to make trade arrangements and bring about freer trade with the rest of the world I am convinced that the people whom we shall find most opposed to that freer trade are the very people who are supporting the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario. I have already seen signs of that in the Financial Post, in a statement to the effect that we in Canada could not expect to accept imports to pay for our exports, that the exports would have to be paid for by Canadian loans. There may be certain ways in which that can be done without giving our goods away, but if there are such ways I do not know of them. I do not believe that there are any. If we do not accept either directly or indirectly value for value for the goods which we export, then we are giving those goods away. I am in favour of discussions and debates on this matter, but there are certain fundamental facts which we shall have to keep continually in our minds while those discussions are being carried on.

I find myself in accord
with what the last speaker has said. I could not help but be amazed at the implications of the statement of the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario. Every once in a while we hear members of the house talk about a large national income and the comparatively small population of the country. They emphasize the fact that it would be impossible for a small population to consume the total production of the country. Then invariably they bring up the question of wheat and try to make people believe that some hon. members suggest we in this country can consume our total production of wheat. Well, in the first place let us remember that the national income is only around nine billion dollars and the population around twelve million. That works out to an average income of

around $3,000 per family of four. Does anybody suggest that a family of four could not consume an income of $3,000 a year if they had the opportunity? Nobody suggests that we should consume all the wheat we produce, but we do believe that the people of this country can consume the imports that could be brought back to Canada in exchange for that wheat. We feel that that is the right thing to do, and we have an interest in trying to build up large foreign investments as a result of the sale of that surplus wheat, investments that can pay for losses in the future.
I quite agree that we have a moral obligation, resulting from the war, to help countries which have been overrun by the enemy. That is an entirely different question. This bill is of great importance. In involves $650,000,000, in addition to the $100,000,000 already set up under the Export Credits Insurance Act. That $650,000,000 is an amount larger than our total pre-war budget, and yet this measure comes up for consideration late in the session and we are expected to pass upon it in very short order. It is impossible in such a short time, or by the methods at present adopted, to give matters of this financial magnitude the consideration they deserve.
The minister said that the Washington conference was largely a financial conference. 'Finance is but the bookkeeping of trade, and if we are to believe the many dispatches which have appeared in the newspapers in regard to the conference, now long drawn out, in Washington between the British and the Americans, trade certainly has entered into their discussions in- very large measure. As the hon. member for Kamloops and the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario have said, we in Canada are in a peculiar position, because, while not of the sterling area but more largely of the dollar area, we are greatly concerned with the ability of the sterling area to take our goods and to pay for them with goods in return.
Some statements have been made in-regard to whether or not we should have bilateral or multilateral trade. I believe what we need in this country is trade, and whether we get it under one form or another is not of particular concern. What we need is the ability to make goods, to provide jobs for our people, and to have those goods bought and paid for by other countries where necessary and that we get something in return. One thing we have surely learned in the last twenty-five years is
that we cannot receive money in return. The only way that a foreign country can pay for Canadian goods is by our taking goods in return, although that may not be by a pure bilateral process but through a three-cornered movement or otherwise.
Mention has also been made of the fact that perhaps Canada could use some of the labour and materials which will go into the export of goods which will be financed for the time being through this act by using these goods for our own needs. I believe in foreign trade; Canada, as the fourth largest foreign trader in the world, must rely to a large extent upon that means, for our whole economy -our food economy particularly-and our natural resources must find an outlet for the time being in other great population centres of the world, and we must rely therefore on foreign trade; yet foreign trade is never the equal of domestic trade. If we can build up domestic trade, trade which we can to some extent control, we are much better off. Let us make no mistake 'about the bill now before us. It is to finance trade largely with countries outside the sterling area which have been the largest consumers of our products, and which have bought far more from us than we have ever bought from them; yet they were able to balance their accounts through their other world trading. If there are at the present time unsatisfied needs of the Canadian people, and we are now suggesting that we should develop exports in certain directions, and we do not know whether those exports will be of a permanent nature or whether this measure is a mere stop-gap, let us carefully consider in this committee whether or not some of the man-power and materials which would go to the furnishing of these goods might not be better applied, not only in the short run but in the long run, to the production of more housing in this country, to satisfy more of the needs of the people of Canada, and to raising their standard of living.
As I have said, domestic trade is infinitely better than foreign trade. We of course must rely to a large extent on foreign trade, but where we can put the emphasis on domestic trade let us do it rather than encourage stop-gap foreign trade, if that is what this should be.
To revert to my original topic, while we may not have been invited to sit in or to be a partner in the British-American conference at present going on in Washington, and we cannot demand entrance, yet I believe that if suitable representations were made we would not find the door so closed that we should not know what was going on there. The discussions have a most direct bearing on the future

of this country and on jobs for our people. If we are to grant large credits to foreign countries to take our goods for the time being, what are we to get in return? Shall we obtain any assurances that they will give us longterm trading agreements to take certain of our export surpluses, or are we simply going to find, after we have given them a certain amount to tide over the present time, that we have accomplished nothing, whereas we might have been satisfying the wants of our own people?
I point out that this bill is not, as is the UNRRA bill, a contribution for the relief of distressed areas in Europe. This, as I understand it, is purely a business bill having to do with trade relationships. If we find that we cannot export so much of our present and pre-war surpluses as formerly, it will be necessary gradually, and with as little hardship as possible, to reorientate our own economy and provide more things which our own people can use, rather than continue to have these great export surpluses which we now have in certain commodities.
It is very difficult for us, with all the duties we have as members of this house, to give to this measure the consideration to which it is entitled. I believe that we must apply ourselves to this problem, because of the incursion of parliament and government into the activities of the people, their daily lives and their whole economy depending upon government action to some extent, for direction at least. How different that is from the old days, when everyone believed that the less governments had to do with business the better. Now, every party in any parliamentary system has taken upon itself the responsibility for job creation and for the prosperity of the country. We must realize that our duties have changed in nature, and it is about time we changed our methods of procedure. We cannot possibly give this measure the consideration it requires if we are to do it in the formal body of a committee of the house or in the house itself. We must adopt more of the United States system of committees, if you like-perhaps not in its extended form; but we must be able to have before us those who are experts on these particular subjects, those who attend conferences with other nations with whom we aj-e dealing, so that we may have a fair idea of what all the implications are and not just hit the high spots, which often is as much as is done in the house upon the most important measures. I would therefore suggest to the minister that consideration be given to bringing these matters before a suitable committee so that full representations may be

made before that body, and adequate knowledge may be had before we come in this house to discuss such important measures.

subtopic: BILL TO CONFER CERTAIN POWERS UPON THE GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL

speechtext:
The house resumed from Friday, November 23, consideration of the motion of Mr. St. Laurent for the second reading of bill No. 15, to confer certain powers upon the governor in council during the national emergency following the war.
Mr. JEAN-FRANQOIS POULIOT (Temi&-couata):	Mr. Speaker, in the first place I
desire to congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) and the other members of the cabinet who have discussed this important matter with the representatives of the provinces. It is a very great problem that they had to face, and they have come to a certain compromise regarding the distribution of powers between the dominion and the provinces. The subject has been argued, discussed and debated for a long time. Some jurists hold the view that as the jurisdiction of the dominion on the one hand and of the provinces on the other are both exclusive, it is impossible for the dominion and the provinces to come to an arrangement on matters which are not already provided for by the British North America Act, and that any change in the distribution of those powers should be ratified by Westminster; in other words, that the agreement with the provinces to abandon part of their jurisdiction to Ottawa and the decision of Ottawa to abandon part of its jurisdiction to the provinces is null and void unless ratified by Westminster. I shall not argue that point. All I shall say is that I am sure that my colleagues realize the tremendous importance of this legislation.
During the war parliament did not function as it used to before. Its powers were delegated to various bodies and individuals, and the law of the land most of the time was no longer the enactments by both houses of parliament with the sanction of the king; it was instead just an order. Naturally conditions were most difficult, and we were told that it was necessary to act in that way because matters of urgency might arise at any moment. That was a very good explanation in some ways.
I should like to tell you, Mr. Speaker, that as soon as a state of war was declared between this country and certain countries of Europe the member for Temiscouata wrote to the Prime Minister to inform him of the increase in the price of sugar which was then taking place. The reply was that the government

National Emergency
would see to that matter, and the government intended to do it in a way that is unknown to most members of the house. The first intention of the government was to have it done by two members of parliament under the jurisdiction of the then minister of national defence, the Hon. Norman Rogers. Mr. Rogers called two members of parliament to form a committee of internal security,' the purpose of which was many-sided. It was to look after dominion-provincial relations, food, commodity prices, protection against air attacks, and finally a survey of the press and public opinion. It meant that the government wanted to have all those matters looked after by a couple of members of parliament. The only trouble was that the job was too tremendous for any two members of parliament to be able to do. But that was the offer. Those two members declined-they were to be paid a living allowance in virtue of an order in council passed under the War Measures Act-because it was impossible for any two or even three human beings to deal with matters of such magnitude. But the government should be given credit for the offer that was made at that time for the settlement of those difficulties, and also for foreseeing the inflation which would have resulted if no action had been taken by the government at that time to control prices. It was wise to do it, and the government showed foresight. To govern is to foresee, and the government showed foresight by doing its best to prevent inflation.
On the other hand there is always the question of responsibility and control. I remember a long time ago, after the last war, when Sir Henry Thornton was appointed as the big boss of the Canadian National Railways, there was a certain element of the Canadian Press which suggested that Sir Henry should be free from politics, that he should be left alone to earn- on his job as the big boss of the Canadian National Railways. I knew Sir Henry Thornton very well. He was undoubtedly a great man, but he needed the control and supervision of parliament to do what he would have been able to accomplish under wise guidance. A small number of people who represented the yellow spirit of a few individuals in the management of the railway objected to it and told the government. "Now that you have appointed Sir Henry, leave him alone"; and that feeling has continued to exist, even in this house, when we have been told that some people were doing so well and were such great men that we had to give them the reins although they were not responsible to the people.
We have a responsibility to the people. Each member of parliament is a shock-absorber
for all the policies of the government. We are in contact with the people. We meet them every time we go home. They come to us, they tell us their troubles, and then we come here to try to redress wrongs.
Since the institution of parliament there have been two ways for us to correct wrongs. One is by the sponsoring of public legislation by private members, the other is through the control of expenditure. During the war members of parliament were not allowed to present public legislation. Some public bills were moved by private members but they did not go further than the second reading, and all the initiating of legislation, I mean regular legislation, passed by both houses and sanctioned by royal authority, was left to the government.
With regard to the control of expenditure, I have complained many a time about the shape of the public accounts, suggesting that they should include the details of all expenditure, because it is much better for the country when all expenditure is brought to light in detail, even though nobody reads the public accounts-and each one of us must confess that reading them is not as interesting as reading the latest novel. But so long as the figures are given and all the information is available to all persons, not only members of parliament but everybody, those who have made that expenditure are much more careful. Seldom is crime committed- in daylight; it is the darkness of the night that favours crime; and the same principle applies with reference to information which is lacking in the public accounts. We were told that so much work was done on account of what is properly called war effort that it would have been impossible for the king's printer to publish details of all accounts. Here again we fought for detailed accounts, and I pay homage and respect to my hon. friends the members for Davenport and Broadview for their assistance in the matter.
Well now, there is a great distinction between the settlement of dominion and provincial taxation and the prevention of an oncoming crisis in this country. Even though the arrangement which has been reached by the dominion cabinet ministers and the provincial cabinet ministers is splendid, and I assume that it is, and that they have all shown good will, for which I congratulate them, and have done their best to achieve results, I do not see how the proposal which is contained in the corrected bill No. 15 will prevent the crisis which we are bound to expect in this country, on account of the lack of purchasing power of gradually increasing numbers of unemployed. When a man manufactures a
National Emergency

suit, a pair of boots, an electrical fixture or anything else, he applies his skill to do it and to do it well, and he should earn enough money to be able to purchase adequately, because he is entitled to the comforts of life as much as anybody else. If we consider the tactics of some of our large employers we may wonder whether they will not kill the goose which has been laying the golden eggs, by keeping their men at work for too many hours and preventing others from securing work. It is a great problem. As a rule, now, the hours of employment are ten per day. On the other hand there are man who do not work, who have been let go, who may get something for a limited time from the unemployment insurance fund but whose future is far from being bright. They are greatly concerned because their skill is not being put to use at the present time, Others, too, may be laid off and increase the numbers of unemployed. How long will they be out of work? Well, it is the secret of God. But here our duty is to see to it that the wheels of business in this country turn regularly so that the least possible number of Canadian citizens shall be affected by the period of transition which we have reached.
It is very easy to paint a rosy picture of the future. It can be done when someone tries to convince himself by auto-suggestion that conditions will improve. Sir, I may be contradicted in some quarters but I believe that those who are the true representatives of the people are precisely the men who have been elected by the people to enact legislation for the benefit of the people at large. Those men are found here and in the other legislative assemblies of this country, and their duty is not always to consider the accomplished fact. Their duty is to proceed exactly as the government did at the start of the war and even before the war began, with regard to anticipated inflation. The duty of all public men to-day is to prevent the crisis that otherwise will inevitably come. I do not wish to pose as a prophet of evil; not at all. But it is enough to listen to people in all walks of life to know that their hearts are not full of that joy that one could expect after we have won a victory over the common enemy. There is worry in every home; we do not find the exuberant joy that we saw everywhere after the first war. Of course, in many countries in Europe the war is still on. It is the same in Asia; the fires of hate are not yet extinguished throughout the world. Far from it. So much so, that in the bill I hold in my hand it is mentioned that the war is not over. Fortunately it was changed in the new draft Think of it, sir.

After V-E day in May last and V-J day in August the war is still on-most extraordinary. But fortunately it was decided by the dominion-provincial conference that the war will be ovbr on the first of January.
I have some suggestions to offer before I resume my seat, and one of them has reference to the responsibility of members of parliament. We have not only a responsibility for answering the letters that we receive, which is one of our duties, and for acting honestly and fairly with all our electors, which is another of our duties. Our task is much more than that. Foresight is not the exclusive possession of the government. Members from all over the country are here to inform the government about disturbances that may occur in their far distant constituencies. They are here to make suggestions.
My first suggestion is that we put an end to the crisis of irresponsibility. I do not mean ministerial irresponsibility, but clerical irresponsibility, which has been the curse of the country since the beginning of the war. I am ready to give credit to some men who have been at the controls. I am ready to say they have done their best. But my contention is that they would have done much better had they been submitted to the control of parliament and had they not been called supermen, men who cannot make a mistake. With the problem of irresponsibility we have that of infallibility, and in this case it means that those who are not responsible to the people are infallible while those who are responsible to the people are fallible. The latter proposition is just as true as the former is not. We are fallible, of course, but the others are fallible too, and I do not see why members of parliament who are responsible to the electors for all the errors and mistakes of these men should always receive the blame.
We can make friendly suggestions for the improvement of things in this country, but they are always and inevitably turned down, and they are turned down because they come from members of parliament. If any member of parliament who makes a suggestion were a dollar a year man he would be considered a genius. It is precisely because the member of parliament is elected by the people and is responsible to the people that he is not accorded the same degree of confidence and respect as the others are.
It cannot go on like that. I am for the Tudor. system of government and not for the Stuart system. You remember very well, sir, the difference between parliaments under the Tudors and under the Stuarts. The Tudor

National Emergency
kings were friendly to parliament and the Stuarts were not. And how did that struggle end? By the triumph of parliament.
My impression, sir, is that we live now in an atmosphere of illusion. Members of parliament work hard. They are in committees early in the morning and sometimes they sit there during the afternoon, and their work on those committees may be done very conscientiously, leaving them not a moment of leisure. But what purpose does a committee serve? What purpose does any committee serve here as things are at present constituted? Members are bound to make decisions, because if they do not reach a decision there is no agreement and there is no report. And when a report comes in it is put on the shelf to wait for future generations.
My impression of what is done by members of parliament is that each of us could be compared to a horse on a disconnected treadmill. The horse walks all the time on the treadmill but does not advance one inch. It is covered with sweat, but the mill is disconnected and nothing is done, although the horse has .the illusion of accomplishing something. I do not say that to deprecate the work of members of parliament. I have the greatest admiration for my colleagues, but I find that in spite of the enormous quantity of work that is done by each of us we do not achieve the results which we should get, because perhaps we are not taken sufficiently into the confidence of the government in the drafting of policies of national concern.
I do not think that the present system of various boards will help to prevent a dangerous state of affairs in this country. To a certain degree it is a question of taxation. It is not so much a question of restriction as the foremost question of adjusting difficulties between capital and labour in order to settle them.
We are about to contribute to the establishment of an international peace court somewhere in Europe or in Canada. Why not have our own peace court here, a peace court composed of men who are outside of the government and outside of the civil service, men who are free from big business and who will not represent classes?-because the representation of classes inevitably brings about a clash. What we need is the representation of the nation, as we represent it here in parliament. We need a body really independent of government, a body which is not a stool-pigeon of the government or the servant of the government; a body which is entirely free. This body should be composed of men of the soundest judgment, men who will be able to 47696-184
deal with the question of the fluctuations of labour, of wages and even of salaries. It should be a kind of tribunal on which the dominion government as well as the provinces can be represented. They should represent the nation for the benefit of the nation.
There are serious-minded people who think that should be done at the earliest possible moment. Perhaps it is not too early to do it now. Sometimes I have spoken of things that were not believed when I said them, but I now ask my colleagues to think about realities, to think about the things as they are now, and also their trend. I am sure that they agree with me that something has to be done to meet unusual conditions. Moreover it is impossible for any government to find jobs for all the boys returning from overseas. It is impossible for the government to keep in their former jobs all the men who have been working in munitions plants. There are many things that should be done; there are many wrongs that should be redressed. When I think of the boys of the merchant marine who have no preference in the civil service I am ashamed.
How many corrections are to be made? Suggestions may come from any member of parliament, but my suggestion to-day is (hat while this legislation may be needed at the present time, if we are to bring about lasting and favourable results we must adopt,something different at the next session of parliament. I [DOT] do not want my constituents to be the slaves of anyone for a certain number of years. The question is not so much the issuance of permits for tires or the removal of some restrictions as it is the organization of the thing that we should never have departed from-order in society. I distinctly remember that in February, 1939, at the beginning of the session before the war, I mentioned all the speeches that had been made about discipline in England, in the United States and even in Canada. Some of those people who were so strong for discipline were praising Hitler. There was an Anglican archbishop who was praising Hitler. He said that Hitler was a coming man, a man who had a policy that would benefit the world to the utmost. Of all those whom I have mentioned there was only one man who spoke of order, and the surprising thing is that he was the Minister of Finance. He spoke of order in a speech he made in New York.
I am against discipline. If we call for discipline it is because order no longer exists. Our work here should not be for the continuation of discipline of the Canadian people; it should be for the reestablishment of order, which is
National Emergency

the gift of God to man. The men who are not of good will in this country are very few. We must work together for the reestablishment of that order. It cannot be done in one day; it cannot be done in two days or in two months. It should be the work of the future sessions of parliament to see that that is brought about. I say to the government it will be much more important for members of parliament to meet in committee for that purpose than to waste their time discussing the extradition treaty with the United States, a horse on a disconnected treadmill.
I deeply regret that in the first place, so many of those experts do not know how to work. In the second place they lack imagination. In the third place I find that they are imbued with an exaggerated sense of importance, an importance that is attached to them by others. I do not say that to depreciate them too much, but they need control. We are here to control what is done not only by the government but by all the boards which administer Canadian business. There must be a great reform, and that reform must start in this very house, where hon. members must display their sense of proportion and give as much importance to any of their colleagues as to anyone who is not responsible to the people. It was quick and easy to depart from centuries-old tradition; it will perhaps take us a long time to come back, but this is the right way. We shall not find the right road by going farther along the wrong one. We shall . have to retrace our steps to the crossroad, find the right way and then proceed farther along it; and the right way is that which has been beaten by our forefathers. It is the way of ministerial responsibility. We have had some troubles in this country. They always occurred because the government of the day departed from the principle of ministerial responsibility.
I will not say any more for the time being, but perhaps I may do so later on.
I have spoken with great concern about the future, and those who have children will understand my feelings. Most of us are old enough; we do not know how long we will live. Perhaps we shall see the next war, perhaps not. What is to be hoped is that the next war will be put just as far as possible into the future, so that neither the living generation nor their children nor their grandchildren will see it, because when it comes it will be the end of the world. But the end of the world may not only come through the' atomic bomb. There are civil wars that are to be averted at all costs, and this is one of them. Hon. members of the House of Commons should put aside all their

political differences to consider this matter as it deserves to be considered. I hope at this time the government will be broad enough to accept some earnest suggestions offered by a veteran of parliamentary life who has at heart the welfare of his fellow citizens.

Finally, parliament will find itself before a definite situation which it may criticize but which will not have been submitted to it for approval and for which it will be held responsible by the people. The golden age of governmental boards will thus have reached its height. The czars in charge must feel secure; they are and will remain above the law. They are ahd will remain above the representatives of the people. Being accustomed to controlling trade in all its forms and to piy into everybody's business, Mr. Gordon will continue to dictate to everyone, including the provincial legislatures, to dominate the unruly, to prosecute them before the courts and, by way of amusement, to assume the role of supreme arbiter of fashion, and to determine with his learned advisers, the colour, the length and the thickness of ladies' under-garments and men's shirts.
The ineffable wartime prices and trade board has permitted and encouraged, by its untimely interventions and culpable omissions, the manufacturers to abandon the maldng of low-priced articles in favour of [DOT] goods on which they make large profits.
The quality of garments, canned goods, gasoline, has deteriorated but the authorities, however, have not decided to alter the standard prices of the basic period, and this has contributed to an important rise in the cost of living.
Now we come to the selective service. It is an unmitigated conscription system, placing the country's man-power under the grasp of the all-powerful officials who force everyone, 47696-184J
employer and employee alike, to bow to their rulings and comply with their demands. They may tell one of the good people from my constituency that although there is no work for him in his town, there is plenty of it in northern Ontario; that he had better leave his family and go to work as a miner in a place hundreds of miles from his home; or else, there will be no unemployment insurance for him.
Mr. Speaker, the workers in my constituency, who have toiled like galley-slaves during the war and have often received, at the end of the week, nothing better than tax receipts for their pains or cheques reduced by half by fiscal deductions, are tired of these annoyances and vexatious measures. They want work but they also want to remain free to sell their services to whatever employer they prefer, without having to report to a superior whenever they quit a job or take on a new one.
On the other hand, the property owners have had enough of the lessons taught them by the rent administrators during the war and they now wish to be again masters in their own houses and be entitled to rent their properties to whatever tenants they choose. However, the infallible creatures of the government tell them that they may not do it.
What does it matter to me that, in order to gild the pill, some restrictions on a few commodities have been removed and some orders have been cancelled; our people are tired and have had enough of boards of all kinds, who have taught nothing but crime and moral turpitude, by forcing our citizens to resort to all sorts of tricks in order to evade the law and get what they sorely needed.
Bill No. 15 authorizes the governor in council to adopt rules which he deems necessary, according to his liking, iri the fields of production, trade, exchange, transport, etc. It is a blank cheque handed the government, not in order to safeguard the rights and privileges of the ordinary man, the humble citizen, the poor or the masses who have suffered and are still suffering, not in order to allay and reduce the effects of six years of privation, but to preserve in the country a war-like atmosphere which will allow the government to please the brass-hats thirsting for military prestige and the bureaucrats stricken by the evil of internationalism, who want an armed force in time of peace to defend foreign countries in time of war. Our people will have to go without sugar, so as not to displease monopolists who will not import this product from South America in order better to control the market.

We will ration meat so as to send more to certain European countries which buy their wheat in Argentine and their bacon in Denmark, when that suits them, but which gracefully accept gifts in critical times.
The Canadian people have sacrificed a great deal during the war; they have, according to civilian and military authorities, both Canadian and foreign, come forward, since 1939, with a tremendous effort on behalf of the allied cause. A heroic task has been achieved, and we are proud of our soldiers, sailors and airmen who fought that the principles of free peoples might triumph, just as we are proud of our workers, farmers, technicians, engineers and scientists who, in the rear, have given an outstanding performance in keeping our armies supplied with munitions, clothing and first rate services. Our people, to whom we held out bright prospects of paradise on earth in a new era of peace and prosperity, accepted without grumbling every hardship and annoyance, in .the hope that by working and helping to shorten the slaughter, they might the sooner enjoy the blessings of the usual everyday life under normal economic conditions. Unfortunately, at present, they must be satisfied with casting envious glances on our neighbours to the south.
As a matter of fact, as soon as hostilities ended, the United States relaxed their control in order to give employment to a greater number of workers and to make it possible for private enterprise to reach maximum production in a minimum period of time, to attain world supremacy in trade and to compete profitably with other countries on international markets. They have put into practice the saying that "Charity begins at home".
Do you not think that the American republic is setting the example for us? Canada, one of the largest producers in the world, may lose the place she occupies in international trade unless the barriers imposed upon her fcra'de by the various control boards are lifted as soon as possible. Our country's prosperity depends on our export trade and if we want to keep employment at the same level as during the war, we must continually increase production in order to export the greatest possible quantities of goods produced by our workers and farmers.
I am aware that the British government has obtained from parliament the authorization to administer the country in conformity with the War Measures Act, but I am also aware that Mr. Anthony Eden stated in the British House of Commons when Prime Minister Attlee introduced that measure "never before
