Mr. Speaker, I sincerely believe the speech which the honourable member for Chicoutimi (Mr. Gagnon) has just delivered is indeed ill-advised. He is one of the personal friends whose acquaintance I have made in this house and whom I have valued. He has greatly disappointed me.
He discussed in the most superficial way a matter which is most difficult. I do not wish to impute motives to the honourable member and I dare say that the views he has expressed and the way he has expounded them, have originated in the minds of people who do not sit in this house. The hon. member has mentioned the prices which prevail in the United States, in his remarks, he said that there is no control in the United States-That is true, but everyone in this house knows how much during the recent war-and even since the end of the conflict-prices have risen in the United States. They have gone up to such an extent that there has come an economic upheaval which, I regret to say, is evidenced by the constant increase in the number and importance of strikes in the neighbouring country.
Would the hon. member for Chicoutimi (Mr. Gagnon) like to see economic chaos happen in Canada? Did his electors send him to this house for the purpose of holding out to them the prospect of the abolition of controls that were established in the general interest?
I am sure that the hon. member has not thought that his constituents were merely voters to whom he would ask a renewal of his mandate in a few years. I still hope that he has considered them as Canadian citizens who are entitled to economic and social security, and I hope that in this debate, within the next few days, he will repent for having delivered a speech which, in spite of the sympathy and friendship I have for him, I consider as ill-advised.
(Text).
Mr. Speaker, if I understand correctly the mandate which has been entrusted to us, we are here to study the present conditions as well as those we may foresee, and to write the laws which will meet such conditions for the benefit of the people, the whole within the limits of the constitution, the rights of the provinces and the sovereignty of parliament. We are here to meet the economic conditions of the reconversion period with legislation that will enable the people of Canada to go through that period without violent shocks. That is our primary duty.
What are those conditions? How can they be met? And then, what effective laws should be adopted? Those are the questions which I intend to discuss.
What is the present economic condition? May I summarize it in a few words? The supply of goods is far below the demand for goods. Before the war our economic life was governed by the law of supply and demand. During the war the supply of goods and services became so low that some controls had to be established in order to avoid inflation and to distribute adequately the few goods and services available. The situation has not changed since the war ended, and will return only slowly to normal conditions. I quote from the proposals of the government of Canada at the dominion provincial conference on reconstruction:
Rehabilitation of men in the armed services, re-conversion of war plants, relief for areas devastated by war and participation in emergency international commodity controls are all emergency requirements arising out of war and call for continuation of national controls for a temporary period. The requirements and duration of this emergency cannot be defined in advance; they must be continuously examined and dealt with in the light of conditions as they develop.
These last words are very important and must be borne in mind in any discussion of the means of going back to a normal economic life. The conditions must be continuously examined and dealt with in the light of conditions as they develop. That is to say, during the period of reconversion some organization must be set up and given the necessary power
National Emergency

to examine constantly and speedily deal with the requirements of any emergency. Before examining what that organization should be let us go further into detail with respect to the economic situation.
Every member of this house will admit that the danger of economic disturbances and especially of inflation has not disappeared with the defeat of the axis powers. Our prices have been fixed during the war on a basis which is called "the basic period prices". Should the price control be removed suddenly, we would witness an immediate upward surge in prices. The supply of goods is not sufficient; deferred needs have piled up and the accumulated demands would bear a terrible pressure on prices, a pressure which would be even greater than during the war.
Higher prices in other countries are also a threat to our own price level. If the price control were suddenly removed, the prices of imported goods would rise immediately, and a lot of commodities that we export would either disappear from the domestic market altogether or be so dear as to be out of reach of the people.
We must not minimize the terrible pressure on prices caused by the tremendous purchasing power at present held by Canadians. The relaxation of personal income tax announced by the Minister of Finance, together with the gratuities paid to veterans, have also increased the buying power within this country. We have to admit that the danger of inflation is even greater than during the war. Let us remember that it was after the first world war, in 1919 and 1920, that inflation was the strongest and highest.
I have here some interesting figures showing the extent to which retail food prices increased after the armistice in 1918. These figures are taken from a publication of the Dominion Bureau of Statistics entitled: "Living Costs in Canada-1913-August 1939". The price of one hundred pounds of flour in July, 1914, was $3.30; in November, 1918, $6.90; and in the spring of 1920, $8.40. One hundred pounds of sugar'cost in July, 1914, $6.50; in November, 1918, $12.30; and in the spring of 1920, $25. Similar increases occurred in the prices of butter, bacon, milk, coffee, eggs and potatoes. For example, one peck of potatoes in July, 1914, cost 25 cents; the same price in November, 1918, and in the spring of 1920, $1.08.
Are, we ready to take responsibility before the people for letting the same thing happen from 1945 to 1947? If we have inflation, the value of our dollar will decrease. What will be the reaction of the worker if the buying

power of his $100 victory bond decreases to the extent that it will buy only from sixty to six^y-five dollars' worth of the one hundred dollars' worth of the same goods and services that it would have bought at the time he purchased his $100 bond?
And what about our returned men?. Is it not out duty to prepare for them a Canada which is worth living in? According to the booklet published by the wartime information board, entitled "Canada at War", the July issue, 1945, the total number of persons in the armed forces as at December 31, 1944, was 759,879. As of March 31, 1945, a total of 1,800,033 men had at one time or another been in the armed forces. This does not include more than 40,000 women. A large proportion of these have returned or are returning to civilian life as speedily as possible. This means an increased demand for goods of all sorts and for housing. It means an increased drain on domestic food supplies, although it must be admitted that the personnel of the armed forces were largely fed with Canadian food. The effect is much more striking in the case of clothing. Every man knows how difficult it has been during the last year or so to obtain men's clothing. Let us as-sume that, one-third of the population of Canada consists of adult males. Let us assume also that 700,000 discharged men require clothing. This means a sudden increase of from twenty to twenty-five per cent in the demand. Unless price controls are maintained, it requires little imagination to see the possible effect.
By the same token there is' a great increase in the pressure on housing. Many returned men will wish to marry immediately anid set up homes. Many will wish to build homes with their discharge benefits provided for that purpose. Many whose wives lived with parents during the war will now wish to set up separate establishments. Again realizing that not more than onenthird of the population are wage earners and probably not more than one-fourth of the population are actually tenants or occupiers of housing accommodation, the discharge of service men means a sudden increase in the demand of probably close to twenty per cent, and this means increased pressure on rentals, on new houses, on building materials and on furniture.
The control of prices, including the rentals, must be kept in force, otherwise we go directly to inflation, and we, who have the responsibility of legislating for the people as a whole, will be responsible for an economic chaos.

National Emergency
la preventing economic disturbances we have the primary duty to see that the essential needs of the population are satisfied. A sufficient quantity of essential goods has to be either produced or imported and then equitably distributed. Even at present, now that the war is over, some domestic and imported materials are in very short supply, and will be for a time which is impossible to determine. It is understood that large quantities of raw materials will be released and made available as component parts for civilian industries, but the need of the public for such important items as automobiles, electric stoves, refrigerators, et cetera is so widespread that we should see that they were equitably distributed. On the other hand, the shortage of certain imported materials, as fats, oils, tin, rubber, sugar, textiles, will be continued for an undetermined period of time, and will be made worse by the terrible needs of the liberated countries for such supplies. In a considerable number of cases the imports are subject to international agreements. As long as bulk purchasing is necessary on the international markets, purchases have to be made by government agencies.
The same is true of exports. Owing to the higher prices outside Canada it is necessary to regulate all exports in order that some essential goods are not exported to the detriment of internal needs. For example, in normal times Canada does not export textiles to the United States. At the present time their export is controlled. Canadian prices are, however, definitely lower than United States prices. If the export controls were removed, the small quantity of textiles we have would disappear over the border very quickly. Exactly the same thing applies to meat, poultry, timber, charcoal, et cetera. That is why I think, Mr. Speaker, that the words "exports and imports" should remain in any other draft of the bill.
Exports and imports, however, are only one aspect of the problem. Domestic production has to be directed towards the needs of the population, and that means centra! production directions as long as the supply of goods and services in Canada has not reached the level of the demand. Rationing and priorities are still necessary, and will be as long as essential consumer goods are in short supply. It is tiie only way of ensuring their fair distribution.
I respectfully submit, Mr. Speaker, that I have mentioned a few facts rvhich demonstrate that there is still, and for at least one year to come, a national and economic emergency. It is essential for the security, defence, peace, order, welfare and good government of
Canada that all practical measures should be taken to prevent economic dislocation, hardship and suffering to Canada as a whole until such national dangers as the risk of inflation, of shortages, and national maldistribution of essential goods and services have passed. That is why I am going to vote on second reading for the principle of the bill.
As suggested by the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent), we shall have the opportunity of discussing the extent of the powers needed when we study the bill in committee. I repeat now w'hat I said at the beginning, that during the period of reconversion some organization must have the power to examine constantly and speedily deal with the requirements of an emergency. What should be the organization?
The British North America Act distributes the legislative powers between parliament and the provincial legislatures. The British North America Act is a bilateral contract, and one party to it cannot ask the other to surrender some of his rights for a certain period of time unless he is ready to do the same when it is necessary for the good of the other party. In certain exceptional circumstances it has to be done, either by one party or the other for the benefit of all. I am a strong believer in the confederation pact, and I hold that neither party should be asked at any time to surrender some of its rights in the political field, but I am ready to admit that under certain emergency situations, one party may ask from the others the surrender of certain rights and privileges in the economic and social fields. It is in virtue of that principle, which acts reciprocally, I repeat, that some of the provincial legislative powers on given matters have to be surrendered to the dominion parliament in a time of emergency to attain, through central laws and regulations, economic stability for our country as a whole. Unless such ..laws or regulations are uniform and enforced in a uniform way throughout Canada, there will be chaos similar to that which we should suffer without any control at all. No one will pretend that such uniformity could be attained now through all the provincial legislatures or governments.
If the power to fix maximum prices on all commodities were left to the provinces, I submit there would possibly and even probably be unrestricted competition between provinces. For instance, the automobile industry is exclusively located in Ontario. Nothing could prevent the legislature in Toronto, or the provincial government, from raising the prices of automobiles and trucks for the benefit of local industries or to permit such industries to raise wages of workers in order to avoid strikes, for example. Let us admit that
National Emergency

at least the temptation would be great. What would happen in Ontario would normally carry reactions and retaliation from other provinces on the commodities they produce; and any control of prices would be tom to pieces. But let us admit for one moment that it would be possible for all the provinces to reach an understanding in order to keep prices down. It would be at the cost of nine different price administrations and enforcement offices, at the cost of constant interprovincial conferences held by hundreds and thousands of representatives, even if there were' only one for each field of commodities, everyone trying to get the most for his own province. I am drawing in my mind a picture of these thousands of representatives meeting together somewhere in a large room, and I ask hon. members of this house to picture for themselves what a Capharnaum it would be. But price control is. not all. Let us suppose that the provinces reach uniformity of price control. What about supply and distribution? The normal course for each province would be to try to satisfy the province's demands before selling elsewhere in Canada. Butter, which is in short supply, is produced mostly in the west. If the prairie provinces satisfied all their people's needs before selling elsewhere, some people in Canada would be completely deprived of all commodities.
The same is true for maple syrup produced only in Quebec. It is true also for the automobile industry located exclusively in Ontario. How would the citizens of the rest of Canada like to look at our friends from Ontario driving beautiful and brand-new cars while they themselves would be walking? These things would certainly happen if the control of supply and distribution were provincial. The provinces might try to reach some agreement and we would witness between them the bargaining which has caused the ruin in the Balkan states, not to mention that the procedure would be so slow that the shortages would be over when the agreements were reached.
Our economy is a complete national whole and any control of it has to be one and must apply to Canada as a whole. Uniform economic control by the provinces is a Utopia. I am a strong advocate of provincial autonomy; I am not a centralizer; but I have to be practical. I would ask Ihose who hypocritically shout about provincial autonomy in everything whether they are ready, before the people of their own province or even of their own riding, to take the responsibility for economic chaos. The constitution provides for the temporary transfer of rights in a time of national emergency and the present emergency

is as serious for Canada's economic structure as the emergency of war was for its political structure. If the emergency regulations are to be enacted by the federal authority I now ask the question, are they to be enacted by parliament.
The British North America Act gives the legislative power to parliament and executive powers to the governor in council. In law it would be the right of parliament to enact all regulations on prices, imports, exports, supply, production, distribution and so on. But from a practical point of view, how could parliament, with its slow and complicated procedure, enact the hundreds of orders which would be necessary in the period of one year provided in the bill? How could parliament be ready at every moment of every day to face any economic emergency which is apt to arise at any moment?
Since the creation of the wartime prices and trade board there have been almost six hundred formal orders issued by the board and almost 1,800 administrative orders issued on behalf of the board. It is true that at the present moment there are only a few hundred basic orders in effect. The number that has been enacted in the past, however, illustrates the complexity of controls generally and the need of continued revision and change as conditions change. One has only to look at a few orders and regulations of the past years to realize the amount of detail involved in control legislation, and consequently the impossibility of parliament itself handling controls by ordinary statutes.
Nothing is dearer to my heart than the sovereignty and the rights of parliament, but is it not our duty under the emergency circumstances to delegate part of our legislative rights to the government and those boards which are in -a better position than we are to deal with the matters mentioned in the bill? As has been said by the member for Chicoutimi the government and its agencies have successfully maintained the Canadian economy during the emergency of war. The wartime prices and trade board, for example, has accomplished a tremendous and wonderful job. Canada stands first in the world for its record in the struggle against inflation. Who wants now a programme of free competition which would, under the present conditions of lack of supply, lead us directly to high self-pricefixing by monopolies and cartels?
The only practical and possible solution at this moment is to surrender to the government part of our legislative powers. Let us not exaggerate. After all, the government is always responsible to parliament for all its acts and those of its boards, agents and con-

National Emergency
(rollers. Whenever parliament is not satisfied with the government's actions, it may reverse the government at any time.
I have already said that I am going to vote for the bill because I deem it essential that we surrender our legislative powers to 'the government in certain definite maters, but I do not feel that I have the right to do more than give the government such legislative powers as are necessary to meet the emergency situation. I do not feel that the people of my constituency gave me a mandate merely to pass that mandate over to the government.
I eannot accept without explanation section 5 of the bill introduced in the house on October 5-section 4 in the new proposed bill which will be studied in the committee has the same meaning. In that respect I am not far from the opinion expressed on Friday, November 23, by the hon. member for Lake Centre, which I quote at page 2457 of Hansard:
That section means that all the orders in council that have been passed since 1939 will, on the day that this bill becomes law, be deemed to have been enacted by parliament and to be thereafter in effect.
The hon. member went on to say:
Section 5 ratifies everything that the government has done under the War Measures Act and all the orders in council in effect on the date when this hill becomes law.
Further on the same page the hon. member said:
I repeat, under section 5 parliament^ is asked * to give approval to orders in council passed under the War Measures Act, sight unseen, in some cases unheard of by parliament.
Further on in his speech the hon. member said:
Under the guise of giving support to certain controls we are asked to stand up manfully in this parliament and say to the government: We place our approval on everything that your controllers and ex-controllers, your boards, agencies or commissions have done under the War Measures Act whether we know of their existence or not.
I understand it is necessary, in order to avoid chaos, that the orders now in effect remain in force. But if the governor in council has taken the responsibility of enacting them, he should also take the responsibility of reenacting them under this bill.
Is section 5 necessary? Could not the governor in council renew the now existing orders on January 1, 1946, or even issue only one order in council which would state that all orders issued under the War Measures Act are reenacted? Could not the governor in council do it under a paragraph which could be drafted as follows-I understand that I have not the right to say that it is paragraph (e) of subsection 1 of section 2 of the new bill:
Continuing, and discontinuing in an orderly manner as the emergency permits, measures adopted during and by reason of the war.
There is another point to which I should like to draw the attention of the house, namely, the possibility of the existence in the bill of a section under which the senate alone could jeopardize the whole economic structure of the country without the consent of this house. It might be argued that under this bill the government will be passing legislation which in ordinary times would necessitate the consent of both houses, and that consequently the withdrawal of the consent of one house only should be necessary to annul any legislation so passed. But it may be answered that if both houses in adopting this bill consent to surrender some legislative powers to the government, only both houses can withdraw such consent, even if it is on one specific matter.
If there is an emergency situation, and I believe there is one, can we take any risk even with the senate? I will go further and say that we cannot take the risk that any order enacted under this legislation after serious study by the cabinet and men of the trade concerned should be pdvoked by the senate, which is not a body responsible to the people, to the detriment of our economy. No order should be repealed without the consent of both houses and after thorough study. There are some means of assuring such an end, and at the same time of safeguarding at least in part the sovereignty of parliament. A joint committee of both houses could be set up which could examine, through subcommittees if necessary, the regulations and orders of the governor in council and the boards, and promote a gradual and yet as speedy decontrol as is wise in the national interest.
Decontrol is going to be a difficult job as far as prices are concerned. Let me quote from page 15 of the reference book on economic controls:
The decontrol of prices will involve some risks. This is particularly true of retail or "final purchaser" ceilings since these represent the ultimate line of defence. It is not easy to judge when price control over a single commodity can be safely removed-the appearance of some unforeseen obstacle to the expansion of production or some unexpected increase in demand, possibly resulting from a shortage of another commodity used for similar purposes-might result in a substantial price increase. Moreover, the removal of price control over a particular article is likely to lead to prompt demands for freedom of bargaining on the part of producers of similar or competitive .articles, which would obviously become very strong if the price of the released article rose above its former ceiling while manufacturers of competitive products were still held
National Emergency

to their ceilings. Even if there were no significant price increase for the released article, the freedom to rearrange the price structure concerned, untrammelled by basic period prices, would be regarded by many manufacturers still subject to price control as a very real advantage. There is the further difficulty that ceilings once removed would be extremely difficult to reimpose both from an administrative and public relations standpoint.
It is true, however, that on all procedures of decontrol in all fields parliament should have something to say, and the proposed committee could safely do the work through subcommittees for the various kinds of controls. Why not have, as in the United States, a special committee on economic planning and policy? Such a committee, given the necessary powers to report on government and board regulations and orders, and procedure of decontrol, could at the same time assemble further material for the preparation of still more definite plans for Canada's economic future under normal conditions.
Let me say that we cannot dive into the future, into the dark of the unknown and risk the obligation of finding expedients when a sudden storm arises as we sail on the sea of laissez-faire. Wre cannot go blindfolded to a return of the economic conditions of 1930-39. Some planning has to be done.
If I am for individual freedom, I am against the abuse of it. I am against the unavoidable disappearance of economic and social freedom and security in a world of laissez-faire. I do not mean that government controls should remain when supply and demand are normal. I do not mean that the provinces should not get back their complete autonomy and parliament its complete sovereignty. But parliament has the responsibility of looking ahead to normal times. It has the duty of planning Canadian economy and enacting laws to avoid the errors and faults of a regime which many hypocritically call free enterprise, but which due to such errors and faults is apt to bring about a real enslavement of the people through monopolistic and cartel methods.
To conclude in a few words, Mr. Speaker, we need government economic control for the period of reconversion. We need planning for the future in order to attain two main objectives for the people of Canada: one, the establishment and maintenance of world and interior peace; and two, the provision of a higher standard of living and of economic and social security for all Canadians.
Mr. JOHN T. HACKETT (Stanstead): Mr. Speaker, to repel the onslaught of totalitarian peoples, Canada found it necessary to adopt their methods. At this moment we are en-

deavouring to extricate ourselves from the situation created by these methods. May we hurriedly review the situation? When war came, the dominion government invaded the provincial field, and the cabinet took over the law-making for the dominion. The invasion of the provincial field by the dominion was carried out under an interpretation of the constitution. It was held that in the emergency of war the dominion had power over matters which normally fall within the provincial field; and under the War Measures Act the cabinet assumed powers which ordinarily reside in parliament to legislate for the people of Canada.
The war is over. During the emergency of war the War Measures Act gave powers which are mentioned in sections 3, 4 and 5 of that act; but the emergency came to an end when the war was over; the validity of all orders in council enacted since the end of the war may be properly questioned under section 6 of the War Measures Act, which says that the act shall avail only as long as the state of war exists. If anyone doubts this proposition he has but to turn to the preamble of bill No. 15, where it is so stated in terms.
What is to be done to get the Canadian people back to normal methods of government? Bill No. 15 has been brought down. It declares frankly that an emergency exists other than an emergency arising from war. There has been brought into this house and distributed to hon. members another bill No. 15, which I will style the second edition. It has been stated that it is not competent to hon. members to discuss the second edition of this bill until it has been introduced. I doubt very much if that be the government's wish. It is quite apparent that the government found that for reasons good or bad it could not maintain the position it took in bill No. 15, first edition, so that it caused to be distributed bill No. 15, second edition, as an intimation of its intentions. I assume-that it was to preclude the necessity for two debates that bill No. 15, second edition, was made available to hon. members, in order that they might direct their remarks to the legislation the government intends to enact, provided that the second edition of the bill does not meet with the same sorry fate that was meted out to the first edition.
I do not think, Mr. Speaker, we need be very much disturbed in discussing the secqnd edition because, with the exception of section 3(g) of bill No. 15, first edition, which is something in the nature of a combination of a naturalization act, an immigration act and an extradition treaty which would confer

National Emergency
upon the executive power to deal in stringent fashion with people in the country as well as those who wish to come into it, the terms of the second bill in the result are identical with those of the first. Possibly with this exception, that bill No. 15, first edition, is clear; everyone understands what it means. Bill No. 15, second edition, is confusing; it has succeeded in confusing everyone a little.

subtopic: BILL TO CONFER CERTAIN POWERS UPON THE GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
Possibly the minister
has had more experience with confusion than I have had, and I will let him speak to that point. But I would ask him to listen for just a moment, and perhaps he may have an opportunity later on to explain what this means. In bill No. 15, first edition, we find there is an emergency; here is the language: ... the War Measures Act be continued in force and that the governor in council be authorized to do and authorize during the said period such further acts and things and make such further orders and regulations as he may by reason of the national emergency resulting from the war deem necessary or advisable . . .
The second edition is not quite so clear. It is in these terms:
. . . and certain orders and Regulations made under the War Measures Act be continued in force and that the governor in council be authorized to do and authorize such further acts and things and make such further orders and regulations as he may deem necessary or advisable by reason of the emergency and for the purpose of the discontinuance, in an orderly manner as the emergency permits, of measures adopted during and by reason of the emergency . . .
Now that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) has composed some of the great difficulties with which he has been confronted, I wish he would turn a few moments of his leisure when opportunity offers to the paragraph which I have just read and enlighten the house as to its meaning. There are a few of us who are perplexed by this multiemergency, which seems actually to mean that there is and there is not an emergency. If I grasp the significance of the terminology, it means that there was an emergency, that there is not an emergency now, but to retreat from the emergency we must have emergency powers. That is what I believe the bill means.
If there be an emergency, it is not a war emergency. If there be an emergency, it is an emergency which arises from the totalitarian legislation which we enacted to fight and defeat a totalitarian people. That distinction is important. A system of controls can be effective only in so far as it is allembracing. We have it on the high authority
of the minister who said at page 2452 of Hansard: "That the whole of these controls are integrated, and each part is necessary to the harmonious functioning of the whole system." If it be necessary to maintain all the controls in, order that they may function and we have an emergency arising out of the operation of these controls, I submit that it is futile to perpetuate controls for the purpose of releasing ourselves from controls. It does not make sense.
I do not criticize those who had the responsibility of enacting the legislation that brought these controls about. They were anxious to win the war. They had but one aim in view, and they have achieved that aim. But to achieve it they paid a price. I say to the hon. member for Montmagny-L'lslet (Mr. Lesage) that the Canadian people paid a price which is spelled out in liberty and freedom and that a price in that coinage is too high to pay for anything but life itself. When we come to consider our present situa-ton and determne what course we should follow, we cannot hope to get back to normal without going through some turbulence, without experiencing some inconvenience. Anybody who takes a stimulant, anybody who develops artificial energy within himself must pay a price and Canada just cannot afford to taper off in a matter of this kind.
I submit that the emergency which confronts Canada to-day is not a war emergency ; it is an emergency which arises out of the legislation which we enacted to win the war. We cannot ease ourselves out of it, because that is impossible. You cannot dam half a river; a dam to be effective has to go all the way across. I would draw to the attention of the house the fact that bill No. 15, whether it be edition No. 1 or edition No. 2, goes farther than the War Measures Act. It reenacts everything that was passed under the War Measures Act and it adds everything that was forgotten or omitted in framing the War Measures Act. We are told that this is being done for the purpose of maintaining order.
Somebody has threatened us with terrible trouble, with great evils, unless these controls be continued. What are these great perils? The hon. member for Montmagny-L'lslet tells us that flour went up, that sugar went up in price. Supposing it did; supposing it goes up again. Is that to be weighed on the same scales with the intolerable situation in which the Canadian people find themselves now that the war is over? I submit that the control of prices is the first step in the first mile toward a situation which makes of a
National Emergency

whole people so many vassals. That may sound somewhat extravagant, but anybody who is inclined to examine the situation, anyone who is inclined to find out just what it means to curtail the freedom of buying and selling, just what it means to those who are subjected to it, will not question the accuracy of that statement.' If you control prices, of necessity you control wages. When you control prices and wages, you determine where men are to work. When you determine where men are to work, you tell them that they are to leave the province of Quebec to go to another province to earn their bread. They are no longer free; they are bound to accept dictation; they are bound to accept the rule of some master. Who he may be matters little; it is an infringement upon liberty and upon the right of the individual to make his own selection and live his own life.
Not infrequently we hear it said in the house that this is done in Great Britain, that something else is done in the United States. I do not think such instances are very helpful, because conditions are entirely different in Great Britain and in the United States. In Britain the area is much smaller; the British are a homogeneous people, and they have but one legislature. The Americans have a different form of government. We forget that we have in this country nine legislatures with definite' functions, nine legislatures that came into existence to meet the needs of this country. When we are told that some ogre is going to pounce upon the Canadian people and squeeze its life-blood from it if these controls be not reenacted, if cabinet controls be not continued, I wonder whether one has thought that there are competent and going legislative bodies in each province across this country which can look after, as it is their duty to do, the welfare of the people in their respective provinces. Are rental controls required in Prince Edward Island? I do not know. Are they required in Saskatchewan?' I do not know. But I venture to say that the rental situation may not be as acute or as difficult in Prince Edward Island or in Saskatchewan as it is in Ontario and Quebec. Ontario and Quebec have legislatures competent and well able to deal with these situations. I for one think they should not only be permitted but be obliged to deal with them. Let the provinces take up their duties. That is the scheme under which the dominion came into existence. It is well that we should decentralize the power which has gradually been concentrated and kept in the dominion cabinet.

If a man should come back to parliament after having been out of Canada, say on an extended trip to Mars, for fifteen or* twenty years, and witness the degradation, the desuetude, the complete abnegation of parliamentary functions, he would be amazed and wonder what had happened to the Canadian people.
Gradually and because of the existence of war parliament has entrusted its lot to the cabinet. The cabinet has enacted something like one hundred thousand orders in council. But we are not dealing only with the cabinet. I doubt if there is a cabinet member in the house to-day who could put up his hand and say that he had not been embarrassed by the autocrats who have drafted orders in council that he has not had time to read and have enacted laws of which he knows little or nothing. There has grown up in this country, in this city I might say, a body of autocrats who are making legislation for the people and who are telling the harried members of the government opposite: Oh, if you relax these controls even the least little bit, great and irreparable damage will be done to the country, find there will be no remedy because we shall all be swept into the gulf-of oblivion possibly. I for one do not believe that. I am of those who think we took the right course during the war. But as Francis Thompson has said:
Nothing begins, and nothing ends;
That is not paid with moan,
For we are born in other's pain,
And perish in our own.
We shall perish in the anguish that is-brought upon us, not by the war, but by the measures to which we resorted in order to win the war, unless we exhibit that measure of energy which enabled us to win the war to rid ourselves of the shackles that are fastened upon us at the present time.
I cannot do more than point out to the house that these emergencies do. not come from the war. They are indirectly incidental to it. There is no hope of getting away from them, because they cannot be effective unless they are all maintained, and we are only deluding ourselves if we perpetuate this type of government.
Power does something to people. It does something to good people. It does something to decent people. I do not know that I can describe exactly what it does to them, but it certainly warps their point of view. It certainly raises themselves vastly in their own esteem, and it certainly has a tendency to diminish any appreciation of their own fallibility. We have consented that we be governed

National Emergency
for the period of the war with absolutely blind confidence in the righteousness and virtue of those upon whom power was conferred. That was the proper thing to do. But just as it was the proper thing to do then, it is just as much our duty now to react against the philosophy and doctrine of those who preach that Canada will disintegrate and crumble if the We shall perish in the anguish that is brought upon us, not by the war, but by the measures to which we resorted in order to win the war, unless we exhibit that measure of energy whicn enabled us to win the war to rid ourselves of the shackles that are fastened upon us at the price of flour goes to $6 a barrel or if the price of sugar is raised. There are some things that are not measured, as I said earlier in my remarks, in terms of the market. We did not compute our position in that way at Dieppe. We did not compute in dollars and cents our position through the whole period of the war, and I submit that at the present time it is folly to endeavour to do so. I consider that many members of the government, who are just as much devoted to Canada as men can be, are being led astray by the whisperings of those on whom they had to rely during the past five or six years.
We have heard a lot about democracy of one kind and another. It has been described as an especially European form of government. Until recently it was assumed to be the form of government best suited to all civilized peoples, and there was an implicit belief that it was destined' ultimately to triumph over all other forms of government and become itself the vehicle of the permanent golden age. But recent experience and the long story of history go to prove, on the contrary, that democracy is an unstable and impermanent system of government.
Thirty years ago a dictatorship was thought to be merely a passing unpleasantness and anarchy a brief catastrophe. The truth, which is now more evident, shows that dictatorship has been the most lasting of all methods of ruling civilized people and that if the history of anarchy were written it would be shown to have existed for much longer periods than democracy itself. Like the highest and most effective type of citizenship, democracy is a delicate flower of short life. The reason for this comparative impermanence of democracy is plain enough. Like civilization, demopracy is a difficult enterprise, a complex and subtle way of life. Autocracy, the way of the order in council, on the contrary is the easiest and safest way for humanity when the high and more dangerous form of government has broken down. It is a short-cut for civilization to rescue itself from anarchy.
Mr. Speaker, what we require here, what Canada requires is not more legislation continuing controls. What Canada requires is an energetic government, a government with nerve enough to remove controls and give Canada back to democracy and democratic institutions.
Mr. MAXIME RAYMOND (Beauhamois-
Laprairie) (Translation): Mr. Speaker, we are called upon to vote the second reading of bill No. 15, as submitted to the house by the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent), on November 23 last, and to scrutinize the reasons he enumerated in support of the measure. Indeed, as mentioned a while ago by the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett), there has been a second edition. However, whether we consider the first or the second versions, we have to draw the same conclusions, for the difference is in form rather than substance.
The object of this bill seems evident. Since the outbreak of war, the government, under a statute known as the War Measures Act, may, by orders in council, be entrusted with powers which, in peace time, come under the jurisdiction of the federal parliament or the provincial legislatures.
Now that the war is over, the government wish to be entrusted, in peace time, with the same powers, under a different formula. To my mind, this measure has a dual aspect, both dictatorial and constitutional, and it is from these two viewpoints that I intend to consider it.
First, the dictatorial aspect: as I have already pointed out, due to the war, the government has assumed the functions of parliament and governed by orders in council. For six years we have been under a real dictatorship. We had reasons to believe that the war being over this system would come to an end. But no, it is intended that it will be maintained. One has only to read this bill to be convinced of this. It is truly an attempt to establish dictatorship in peace time, in spite of the constitution. It is a flagrant denial of responsible government.
I do not claim that, in certain cases, a measure of control may not be resorted to for a time, but then, let the government ask us to consider a legislation covering specific cases, let them prove to us the necessity of taking such a course, let them demonstrate that these powers are not devolved on the provinces, or that they are unable to exercise them; then we shall be in a position to decide with full knowledge of facts. But we are asked at the present time to give a blank cheque without being shown sufficient reasons for doing it.
National Emergency

However, we know how the government intend to exercise these powers. We all remember that, a short time ago, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) who was then acting prime minister told us, in support of his refusal to table orders in council, that it was up to the minister to decide whether it was in the public interest to supply these orders to the house and that the house had to be governed by his decisions.
Never had such an autocratic and dictatorial pronouncement been uttered in this house.
Just imagine, Mr. Speaker! While parliament is in session, the cabinet legislates by order in council, and the assembled representatives of the people are not even entitled to information about this legislation which belongs to parliament. If that is not dictatorship, I do not know the meaning of the word.
Never in peace time has a more antidemocratic measure been introduced in parliament.
After a six year war which proved tremendously costly in life and wealth and which was waged, we were told over and over again, to overthrow dictatorship and to defend democracy in Europe, the most anti-democratic measure one could possibly devise is introduced. What a joke!
What is even more astounding is that such a bill should be introduced by a Liberal government, headed by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King).
On August 2, 1935, before the general election held the same year, the Prime Minister expounding the Liberal philosophy in a broadcast speech to the Canadian people in which he criticized the legislation put through by the Bennett government during what were perhaps the most critical years in our history- unemployment at that time endangered the economic future of the country-spoke as follows:
Restoration of Responsible Government
The Liberal party believes that the present crisis has been made an excuse for the usurpation of the rights of parliament, and the assumption of autocratic powers by the executive. Liberalism stands, as always for the principle of a free parliament, and for the supremacy of parliament. To this end it would repeal the legislation enacted by the present administration, which deprives parliament of its control over expenditures and taxation, and invests the executive with unwarranted arbitrary powers, as for example:
(1)	legislation permitting the executive to enact measures by order in council for peace, order and good government, and
(2)	legislation providing the executive with [DOT] "blank cheque" for expenditure of any kind.

What the government alleged to be emergency measures, to aid in the relief of the unemployed, have turned out to be a part of a deliberate policy, directed -towards accustoming the public mind to the framework of the fascist state. We cannot too soon, once more, subject the executive to the control of parliament, if we are longer to have responsible government in Canada.
No better qualification could be applied to this bill or help us weigh its merits. These words I commend to the consideration of the house.
Some of the absolute powers the government seeks come under dominion jurisdiction while others are provincial prerogatives.
Let us first look into those which may be delegated by the dominion parliament. We will then discuss the others in relation to the constitutional aspect of the bill.
What reason has the Minister of Justice alleged to justify the section of the act which deals with the powers of the federal government? None whatever.
Of course, he said, without proving it, however, that a state of national emergency prevailed, but that was mainly to justify the government's encroachment upon provincial rights.
Parliament was assembled on September 6 to pass the legislation needed to meet present conditions.
The speech from the throne stated that everything had been foreseen and that, accordingly, plans had been prepared and were already in operation. I quote the following excerpt from the speech from the throne:
So far as the future could be foreseen, my ministers had taken steps to see that -Canada was prepared to meet the very difficult situations which would arise when victory had been won.
We were told that everything had been foreseen.
Preparations for the demobilization, -rehabilitation and reestablishment in civil life of the men -and women in' the armed forces were well under pray when Germany surrendered. The same is true of -measures foT the reconversion of the economic life of our country from a war-time to a peace-time basis, and for the maintenance of -a high level of employment and national income. The plans thus developed to meet the requirements of the period of transition are now being put into full operation.
In view of those official statements, I do not see any justification for parliament delegating its powers to the governor in council.
More than that, we have been sitting since September 6, ready to pass any* necessary legislation to meet any emergency and I am still endeavouring without success to find any justification for Parliament delegating its powers to the government.

National Emergency
What are the exceptional measures submitted by the government since this session began or since September 6, to meet an emergency?
Certainly not that dealing with a national flag bearing the union jack as advocated by [DOT] the Minister of Justice.
Certainly not that dealing with British nationality under the camouflaged name of Canadian citizenship.
The Housing Act was amended but it was already on the statute books. A special act has been passed to provide for the welfare of returned soldiers.
If other measures were necessary, why have they not been introduced?
There has been a strike in Windsor for the last three months. But when some hon. members brought up the matter in the house claiming that it was urgent, it was held that it was not sufficiently urgent to warrant discussion at that time and the strike is still going on. I wonder what the government is doing with its dictatorial powers to settle the condition prevailing at Windsor?
In short why are we here? In what respects has parliament been unable to cope with the situation? This has not been shown.
But the bill goes farther than that and encroaches on the prerogatives of the legislatures, which is more serious, and that is what induces me to discuss the constitutional aspect of the bill.
If one refers to the bill, he finds that several of the powers specially requested fall under section 92 of the B.N.A. Act and therefore come under the sole jurisdiction of the provinces.
When the government requests the authorization to take over those prerogatives from the provincial legislatures they violate the* constitution.
To justify its actions the government invoke, as it appears from the preamble of the first edition of bill No. 15, a "National Emergency", stating that the security, defence, peace, order and welfare of Canada ate at stake, while in the second edition of the same bill the words "peace, order and welfare of Canada" have been deleted.
I do not know whether unusual changes have taken place since November 23; but what evidently was the basis of bill No. 15 on November 23 last is apparently no longer the basis of bill No. 15 on December 4, that is ten days later.
The "national emergency" invoked in the bill is not proven and we are entitled to ask the Minister of Justice how Canada's national
existence is endangered and what is meant by a "national emergency"; in addition it must be shown that the provincial legislatures are unable to cope with the situation.
Clause 91 of the constitution which formed the basis of the first edition of the bill, expressly states:
It shall be lawful for the Queen, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons, to make laws for the peace, order and good government of Canada in relation to all matters not coming within the classes of subjects by this act assigned exclusively to the legislatures of the provinces.
Now that the honourable the Minister of Justice has deleted the words "peace, order and good government" from the preamble of the bill, I do not know on what grounds he will seek to prove that his bill is constitutional.
I think I can summarize as follows the arguments advanced by the Minister of Justice in support of this bill on November 23 last:
He claims three grounds; first he considers as a legal principle the decision which the Privy Council gave in 1923 in the Fort Frances case; the legislation passed by the United Kingdom for the purpose of conferring certain special powers on His Majesty's government sirjce the cessation of hostilities; the fact that from November, 1918, at which time the first great war came to an end, to May and July, 1920, the cost of living and wholesale prices indices rose considerably, a thing which might occur again and would constitute a national emergency.
Let us examine the first argument, of a legal character, based on section 91 of the B.N.A. Act and on the Fort Frances case.
(a)	It should first be noted that the above mentioned case related to control powers on the supply of paper, that is one commodity only, which is entirely different from the present case in which the provinces are to be deprived of most of their prerogatives.
Thus, in paragraph _(c) of section 2 of the reprinted copy of bill No. 15, which corresponds to paragraphs (d), (e) and (f) of section 3 of the original bill, mention is made of a number of matters, besides the others that are included in the other paragraphs of the same section.

speechtext:
It is up to the minister to prove that, and that is why I am discussing the reasons which the Minister of Justice has put forward in support of his measure. If the hon. member will kindly wait, I shall come to that later when dealing with the third reason
National Emergency

which the Minister of Justice has adduced jn order to show that a special emergency existed. I am now discussing his first legal argument, namely his reference to the Fort Frances case.
(b)	Besides, the Fort Frances case more especially related to the validity of the war measures act, which has nothing to do with this discussion.
(c)	As regards the principle expounded in :.he above mentioned decision, to the effect that parliament is in a better position than the tribunal to determine the special circumstances creating a national emergency, I may say that the privy council did not hesitate to declare ultra vires certain acts that had been passed by parliament under section 91 of the B.N.A. Act, on the grounds of peace, order and good government, especially in 1921 and 1925 in connection with the Board of Commerce Act, 1919, and the Combines and Fair Prices Act, 1919, as well as in the Snider case. I shall quote from the decision given in 1925 in the Snider case. It was then ruled:
The act could not be justified under the general power in section 91 to make laws for the peace, order and good government of Canada, as it was not established that there existed in the matter, any emergency which put -the national life of Canada in unanticipated peril.
We have there the proof that parliament can decide one way while at the same time the privy council can take an opposite stand. Therefore the legal authority of the Minister of Justice, based on the Fort Frances case, no longer applies, because not only in 1925 but even in 1937, as the Minister of Justice is aware, since he was representing the [DOT] government, the privy council put aside parliament's conception of a national emergency when it invalidated the social legislation passed under the Bennett government in 1934 and 1935 on the grounds of "peace, order and good government".
But I would add, in connection with the Snider case, Justice Duff's remarks, when he declared that "social legislation" ultra vires:
The legislation in question there was framed for the purpose of dealing with industrial disputes and authorized the Minister of Labour to take steps to convene, in the case of such a dispute, a board composed of a representative of the workmen, a representative of the employer. and a third person, to be nominated by the Minister of Labour himself. The act prohibited a strike or lockout pending the consideration of a dispute by the board. The importance of the matters dealt with by the statute, the fact that the statute was making a provision for meeting a condition which prevailed throughout the whole of Canada, and for dealing with industrial disputes which, in many and, indeed, most cases, would affect people in more than one province, the fact that the

machinery provided had proved to be a valuable instrument in the interests of industrial peace, were not disputed . . .
Nevertheless, the board negatived the existence of the general principle that the mere fact that dominion legislation is for the general advantage of Canada, or is such that it will meet a mere want which is felt throughout the dominion, renders it competent if it cannot be brought within the heads enumerated specifically in section 91.
As I have just said, as recently as 1937, the Privy Council ruled ultra vires the laws enacted by parliament in 1934 and 1935 under the Bennett government, at a time when unemployment was at its height.
At all events, that principle does not exempt the government from proving the existence at the present time of "a national emergency" endangering the "security, defence, peace, order and welfare of Canada."
Then, the minister mentioned the United Kingdom legislation.
We cannot compare things that do not suffer comparison. Not only does Great Britain's legislation apply to questions of limited import, when compared with those covered by bill No. 15, but conditions are different over there, as the hon. member for Stanstead has just remarked. In Great Britain there is not, as in Canada, a division of powers between a central parliament and provincial legislatures, and for this reason, there is no jurisdictional conflict nor constitutional issue involved.
Moreover, Great Britain, is in Europe, Canada is in America. The disorders which prevail in Europe are inexisteat in this country. In Canada, famine is unknown while it is more or less prevalent in the United Kingdom which depends upon our exports to live
Thirdly, the minister, as reported in Hansard of November 23, mentioned as a condition of national emergency, the possible increase of the cost of living-and this is the only condition he has mentioned-recalling that, after the end of the first great war, that is from November, 1918 to July, 1920, the cost of living index had shown an increase of thirty-eight per cent, while the wholesale price index had risen by fifty-five per cent from November, 1918 to May, 1920.
I shall be content to point out to the Minister of Justice that the Privy Council has decided that such circumstances did not warrant the central authority to encroach on provincial prerogatives. I refer him to the case relating to the Board of Commerce Act, 1919 and the Combines and Fair Prices Act, 1919, heard in November, 1921. This is a direct answer to the allegations of the hon. minister.

National Emergency
I quote the judgment and a few notes reported in 1 App. C. 1922, pages 191, 197, 198 and 200:
The Combines and Fair Prices Act, enacted by the parliament of Canada, in 1919, authorized the board of commerce, created by another statute of that year, to restrain and prohibit the formation and operation of such trade combinations for production and distribution in the provinces as that board might consider to be detrimental to the public interest; the board might also restrict accumulation of food, clothing, and fuel beyond the amount reasonably required, in the case of a private person for his household, and in the case of a trader for his business, and required the surplus to be offered for sale at fair prices; and the board could attach criminal consequences to any breach of the act which it determined to be improper:
Held, that the acts were ultra vires the dominion legislature, since they interfered seriously with "property and civil rights in the provinces," a subject reserved exclusively to the provincial legislatures by section 92. head 2, of the British North America Act, 1867, and were not passed in any highly exceptional circumstances, such as war or famine, which conceiv- , ably might render trade combinations and hoarding subjects outside the heads of section 92 and within the general power given by section 91.
Now I am going to quote the notes of the privy council:
It is to the legislatures of the provinces that the regulation and restriction of their civil rights have in general been exclusively confided, and as to these the provincial legislatures possess quasi-sovereign authority. It can, therefore, be only under necessity in highly exceptional circumstances, such as cannot be assumed to exist in the present ease, that the liberty of the inhabitants of the provinces may be restricted by the parliament of Canada, and that the dominion can intervene in the interests of Canada as a whole in questions such as the present one. . .
And further on:
It has already been observed that circumstances are conceivable, such as those of war or famine, when the peace, order and good government of the dominion might be imperilled of a character in reality beyond anything provided for by the enumerated heads in either section 92 or section 91 itself. Such a case, if it were to arise would have to be considered closely before the conclusion could properly be reached that it was one which could not be treated as falling under any of the heads enumerated.
Mr. Justice Duff, rendering judgment in the cases to which I have already referred, concerning the act enacted by parliament in 1934 and 1935 under the Bennett government, said:
In the board of commerce case the judicial committee had to consider legislation by which a dominion board was constituted and empowered, broadly speaking, to inquire into, and prohibit, profiteering and practices in connection therewith in dealings in the necessaries of life. In particular, the board had authority to regulate the price of such necessaries of life.
The question arose upon a case stated as to the validity of an order made by the board regulating the prices of ready-made clothing in
certain establishments in Ottawa. The validity of the order was attacked by the association of manufacturers concerned and was supported by counsel on behalf of the board and of the dominion. The litigation raised the concrete question inter partes as to the legality of the particular order; and the answer to that question turned upon the answer to the question concerning the validity of the legislation, which it was, therefore, essential to determine. The statute was supported on various grounds and, among others, on the ground that in the year 1919, when it was enacted, the evils of hoarding and high prices in respect of the necessaries of life had attained such dimensions "as to affect the body politic of Canada." Nobody denied the existence of the evil. Nobody denied that it was general throughout Canada. Nobody denied the importance of suppressing it. Nobody _ denied that it prejudiced and seriously prejudiced the well being of the people of Canada as a whole, or that in a loose popular sense of the words it "affected the body politic of Canada." Nevertheless, it was held that these facts did not constitute a sufficient basis for the exercise of jurisdiction by the dominion parliament under the introductory clause in the manner attempted.
This, I believe, is a direct answer to the facts put forward by the Minister of Justice to justify the existence of a national emergency.
After the first world war, ended in November, 1918, the cost of living, as the Minister of Justice pointed out, went up considerably with the increase in wholesale prices. The government adopted an act to control prices, thereby assuming a right which in peace time belongs to the provincial legislative bodies.
The Privy Council decided those were not sufficient grounds to disregard section 92 of the B.N.A. Act. More recently the measures enacted by parliament under the Bennett administration in 1934 and 1935 on the plea of a national emergency were declared ultra vires by the Privy Council because they infringed upon the rights of the provinces, which alone have the power to pass legislation regarding labour agreements, wages and working hours.
The Minister of Justice has not substantiated the preamble of the bill, that is, "the national emergency" which might endanger the security, defence, peace, order and welfare of Canada. That was essential. According to the Privy Council only in an emergency such as war or famine would the federal government be justified to deprive the provinces of their powers.
Well, the war is over and there is no famine. According to the Prime Minister we export "nearly half of all our inspected meat."
In peace time the provinces have the exclusive right to legislate in regard to property and civil rights, in matters of labour or other
National Emergency

contracts and to fix the quality and prices of goods and services. And as the privy council ruled in 1937'
The _ apportionment of powers as between the dominion and the provincial legislatures is one of the most essential conditions, and very likely the most essential one, of the interprovineial pact to which the B.X.A. Act gives effect.
If controls are necessary, they should be exercised under the authority of the dominion or of the provincial legislatures, as the case may be, but within their own jurisdiction. I am afraid that this legislation is a further step leading to the centralization of powers, in order to gradually deprive the provinces of their powers. I am opposed to that.
Let us respect provincial autonomy.

speechtext:
I say that it is an encroachment on the part of the dominion upon the rights of the provinces. This legislation is null and void and ultra vires. I call the attention of the house to section 9 of the original bill which reads as follows:
This Act shall come into force on a day fixed by proclamation of the governor in council and on and after that day the present war shall for the purposes of the War Measures Act, be deemed no longer to exist.
Well, should this bill be passed and subsequently be declared ultra vires, what would be the consequences? It would cease to be in force. More than that, it would be con-.sidered as never having been in force, as it would be null and void ab initio. And all the consequences of the act would disappear at the same time. As section 9 says that, for the purposes of 'the War Measures Act, war shall be deemed no longer to exist from the day that this act shall come into force, the War Measures Act would have continued and would continue to be in force.
Whether this bill is ultra vires or not, we are asked thereby to grant dictatorial powers to the government, and to strip the provinces of their rights.
