subtopic: BILL TO CONFER CERTAIN POWERS UPON THE GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill before us, an act to confer certain powers upon the governor in council during the national emergency following the war, is nothing more or less than an extension for another year of the powers of the cabinet which they enjoyed under the War Measures Act. The proposed act will authorize the governor in council to continue

legislating by order in council, as has been the case during the war. The system proved to be a very useful and convenient instrument in the hands of the government in legislating as it pleased whether parliament was sitting or not. The question before us now is, should this power of the government be extended for another year? My personal view is that it is essential at this time that the governor in council should have a certain amount of power but only to the extent necessary to enable the government' to deal with ordinary routine matters and matters which are truly emergency matters; but unlimited power of the government should definitely be curbed.
I have personal knowledge of the manner in which many of the various controls operate, and I might as well say frankly that there is altogether too much red tape in their administration. I shall give only one illustration, which is a good example of maladministration called the control. Some of these controlling agencies have simply gone the limit. Their chief aim seems to be to control for the sake of controlling and nothing else.
Several months ago I referred to the construction controller the case of a farmer who, by the way, lives in the constituency of my hon. friend the member for Athabaska. This man applied for a permit to build a small hall and a candy store at a country resort. The value of the building was to be in the neighbourhood of S300. The farmer had his own lumber, which was exposed at all times to country fires, and being an amateur carpenter he was going to build the hall himself in his spare time. He owns one or two boats which he hires out, and manages to keep and clothe his family on the income he receives from that source. The construction controller could not see his way clear to grant him a permit "at the present time".
I submit that in- that case there was absolutely no excuse for refusing the permit. The farmer had the lumber and he was going to do the work himself. But no; the controller was on the job controlling for the sake of controlling. I could recite many other cases where similar things have been done. In view of my experience with the various controllers, therefore, I can .only come to the conclusion that many of them control for the sake of controlling only.
Nevertheless I am in favour of some of the essential controls. I cannot, however, subscribe to all these controls being maintained in a wholesale manner, especially when I know the extent to which this power has been abused even during the war. Does one need to mention the various orders in, council

National Emergency
which were passed while the house was sitting? It might as well be said that altogether too many of these orders in council have remained a government secret far too long. True, the ministers try to justify every action of the government, but the fact remains that these numerous orders in council and controls have placed this nation in a strait-jacket, which is an unhealthy condition for an individual or for a nation to be in.
It must be remembered that all this maladministration and abuse took place during the war. But now that the war is over, the people of this democratic nation resent the undemocratic and unreasonable controls. In other words, the Canadian people demand that parliament exercise some control over the controllers.
I did not rise, however, to discuss merely the administrative inefficiencies of the various controls. I rose chiefly to discuss an important principle. I have in mind the unjustifiable [DOT]disregard of the rights of some of our citizens. Apparently bill No. 15, as originally presented, has been or will be withdrawn and with it section 3(1)(g), and I was wondering whether the amendments which the government will propose will cover the objective of section 3(1) (g). I want it clearly understood that I am not objecting to the granting of some power to the governor in council to deal with what are emergency matters and matters of merely routine significance. But we must draw a line somewhere when we deal with naturalized or Canadian-born citizens. Let me point out what I mean.
At the beginning of the war the government under the War Measures Act passed what is known as the defence of Canada regulations. Under section 26A it was directed that all unnaturalized persons born in territories which were under the sovereignty or control of enemy countries on the dates on which Canada declared war on those countries must register with the police and report from time to time to the police as ordered. It is my personal view that persons who were not British subjects and who were nationals of enemy countries should have registered in the interests of the safety of our country. But persons who were born in countries which fell under the pressure of the enemy were wronged when they were ordered to register as enemy aliens. The original order in council revealed that those who framed it had little knowledge of the history and geography of Europe. For instance, former Czechoslovakian citizens were asked to register as enemy aliens after Czechoslovakia was given away to the nazis at Munich in 1938 against the will of its inhabitants. Having thrown them into the clutches of
the nazis we then proceeded to ask persons who originally came from that country and resided in Canada to register as enemy aliens. Whoever conceived that bright idea certainly made us look ridiculous in the eyes of the nations of the world. Eventually representations were made to a committee of this house by Czechoslovakian representatives in Canada, and the Canadian government amended section 26A of the defence of Canada regulations by passing, on February 7, 1941, order in council P.C. 2420. Other representations were made on behalf of other nationals who found themselves in similar circumstances, and eventually all of them were exempted from this registration.
I might mention at this point that the officials who interpreted these regulations did not even know the difference between Austria as it existed before the first great war and Austria as it existed before this war. For that reason, any person whose naturalization certificate showed that he came from the Austro-Hungarian empire was asked to register if he had taken out his naturalization certificate after September 1, 1922.
But that was not by any means the worst thing the government did. The defence of Canada regulations as originally framed applied only to enemy aliens, but later section 26B was enacted by order in council which brought under.these regulations even some British subjects, namely those persons who were naturalized since September 1, 1922, and who were born in territories which were under the sovereignty or control of enemy countries on the dates on which Canada declared war on them. That is the point to which I wish to draw attention in particular.
I also wish to say at this point that it is time we made up our minds whether we are going to trust naturalized British subjects or not after we have granted them naturalization certificates. We cannot continue to suspect and hold responsible every naturalized Canadian citizen for everything which happens in the country from which he came. I certainly object to the idea of permitting anyone to push around any of our citizens, regardless of where they may have come from originally. Should any one break the law, we have the courts of justice to deal with offenders, whether they are of Canadian or any other origin.
I maintain that nothing positive can be accomplished by such orders as those to which I have referred. On the contrary, they can do us a lot of harm, especially when we assist in promoting suspicion against our own citizens. As I have already remarked', if an individual among a group of naturalized Canadians should break any of our laws, whether in time of war or in time of peace, such individual
National Emergency

should be brought before the courts of justice and dealt with as an individual. I maintain that once we grant a person the status of Canadian citizen he must be regarded as a Canadian. We must do everything possible to help our naturalized citizens to feel completely that they are a part of our nation. When we shall have eliminated suspicion and distrust from our midst we shall then have a truly strong and united Canada.
I should like to place on record a paragraph or so from an order in council which was passed by the governor in council on November 2, 1940, amending the defence of Canada regulations. I am placing these paragraphs on record to show what a ridiculous stand was taken and how little we know about our own people. On November 2, 1940, order in council P.C. 6150 was passed. This is the first paragraph :
Whereas the Minister of Justice reports that it has been reported by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police that certain persons who are guilty of technical offences of not registering in accordance with the provisions of the defence of Canada regulations relating to enemy aliens, have been ordered interned under the provisions of paragraph (9) of regulation 25 of the said regulations.
Further down in the order in council I find this paragraph:
That in view of the' fact that certain persons who were not required to register under the original regulations were under .the impression that they were not affected by the subsequent regulation due to the fact that they were naturalized, some of them have been guilty of the offence of failing to register.
In substance, this order in council goes so far as to offer another opportunity to these Canadians, who had been naturalized since September. 1, 1922, to register as enemy aliens, and therefore paragraph 9 of regulation 25 was revoked, and another paragraph 9 was substituted so that these persons -might register within one month after the notice. It further states:
. . . or if he refuse or fail to answer truly any of the questions put by the registrar, or if being registered he fail to report as hereinbefore required or to observe any of the conditions upon which he is permitted to be at liberty, he may in addition to any other penalty to which he may therefor by law be liable, be interned as a prisoner of war on the order of the Minister of Justice or the registrar general of enemy aliens.
As I have stated, the reason I wished to place these two or three paragraphs on record was to show to what extent the government may go in legislating by way of orders in council. It seems to me that, had this matter been brought before the house, the house surely would not have approved any such legislation. I wish to emphasize as strongly 
, as I can that, when we deal with this particular phase of the problem concerning persons who do not happen to have been born in this country, once such persons become, naturalized citizens of Canada we must not entertain any idea of deporting them wholesale, no matter who they may be; because to-day it may be one group of people, and in a year's time or five years' time it may be another group and so forth.
I wish to read from an article that was published in Toronto in News of November 24, 1945. It is not very often that I agree with Mr. Elmore Philpott, because he is inclined to be pinkish, but on this occasion I consider that he has hit the nail on the head. I quote:
When a person acquires Canadian citizenship, either by birth or due process of law, possession of that right should be absolute and inviolable. It might be argued that for certain offences nationality should be revoked from people who have shown themselves unworthy of it. I doubt even that. But, if so, the power should be conferred only on judicial tribunals where the subject would have all the customary protections of British law. It is nothing short of an outrage to propose that the cabinet be given power to discuss in secret session cases involving revocation of nationality. That is nothing more nor less than the *writing into the laws of Canada of one most outrageous feature of the nazi system.
Surely we all recall the dark days of the depression of the thirties when, through no fault of their own, scores of thousands of immigrants to this country were unemployed, the government of Canada arbitrarily deported whole shiploads of them.
If at that time there -had been on the statute books of Canada the arbitrary and outrageous powers now asked in Bill 15, every foreign-born person would have been made liable to secret revocation of citizenship-and deportation without even so much -as the right to say good-bye to friends or even close km.
Bill 15, subsection (G) of section 3, is the most outrageous proposal ever introduced into the parliament of Canada. It should be stamped on and killed so emphatically that all the world will know that the Canadian people want no thin edge of the nazi doctrine wedged into our most sacred laws.
I agree with that view' wholeheartedly, and having chosen to touch upon this very aspect of our legislation, I might say that we have_ too long entertained the view that if a person does not behave we must brand all other individuals of the same race or the same background as being disloyal t-o the country. I hold that once a person obtains his citizenship certificate and becomes a Canadian citizen we should not even dream of revocation. If a man commits a crime he should be punished, but I see no justification for holding a stick over the heads of all those people who do not happen to have been bom

National Emergency
in this country. The governor in council, by passing these various orders in council, has been wielding this stick altogether too long, and for that reason I am bringing this matter to the attention of the house. I am sure the present Minister of Justice will take my remarks into consideration, and I believe that in the future he will avoid the recurrence of similar action on the part of the government.

subtopic: BILL TO CONFER CERTAIN POWERS UPON THE GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
The bill that was presented to us this afternoon differs in some respect from the bill that was introduced in this house on October 5 last. While it limits to some extent the powers which the government sought under the former bill, nevertheless, if it is passed by the house in its present dress, which is somewhat more modest than the dress it previously wore, it will give the government powers which in my opinion no government should possess in the days of peace.
I wish to place myself on record as opposed to the bill. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said in this house yesterday that he understood no exception was likely to be taken to the principle of the bill. Well, if the principle underlying it was that the government have authority for a period of one year to make orders and regulations, when this house was not sitting, to meet any national emergency that might suddenly arise in consequence of the war I would not find it objectionable. But as I read the bill that is not its principle.
As I read this bill the prineipje that underlies it is, that the government shall have dictatorial powers for a period, which is not altogether definite, to carry on a great part of the business of the country by order in council and by regulations when, how and as it sees fit; or, to put it in another way, the principle that underlies the bill is, not to provide for emergencies in peace time but to provide means of continuing government dictatorship now that the war is over.
I am opposed to the government having such dictatorial powers, and unconstitutional powers in times of peace. The War Measures Act gave the government dictatorial powers [DOT]during the war. It gave the government power to do what it thought was necessary for the security and the defence of Canada. It took away the functions of parliament, or a great many of them. It deprived the provinces of many of the rights given to them by the British North America Act.
I do not find fault with the government having such great powers in times of war; there are good reasons why they should have them. But the war is over now and government orders in council and government regulations are not going to help us win the peace, nor are they going to help us maintain freedom, justice and democracy in this country.
I do not suggest for one moment that all controls should be taken away immediately. I believe it is essential that some controls be maintained for a time, but there is a right way and a wrong way of establishing them.
The wrong way, the unconstitutional way, the undemocratic way, is by government orders in council and regulations.
The right way, the constitutional way, the democratic way is by legislation properly introduced into this house, and after it has been discussed and considered by the elected representatives of the people and by the senate, passed by parliament.
Now that the war is over, are there any good reasons why parliament should surrender one of its most important functions, that of legislating, and let the government legislate by orders in council and by regulations on all subjects set out in section 2 of this bill? If there are any good reasons I have not heard them; if there are such reasons I think the members of this house should be made acquainted with them by the government before this bill is passed.
What is a national emergency? It is not defined in the bill and we have not been told by the government what it is. We should be told that; there should be some definition of a national emergency in this bill before we give the government the great power for which it asks.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I said-and
I propose to repeat it now-under our constitution and under our democratic form of government the men and women who are elected to this house by the people throughout the country are supposed to make the laws, and independent judges have the duties of administering those laws.

That, sir, is a principle that should not be lost sight of; it is a principle that should be carefully observed; it is a principle that should be guarded jealously by the members of this house and should not be surrendered in times of peace if we are to have government by, of and for the people.
Every person in this house was elected by the voters of his constituency to make the laws or to assist in making the laws of the dominion. As I say, we are responsible to them at the next election for what we do here. In my opinion we do not keep faith with them or with parliamentary institutions, nor are we true to the principles of British justice, if we fail in our duty in this respect on the ground of expediency or convenience or national emergency, call it what you will, and let the government make orders and regulations which have the force of law and impose fines and penalties for their violation, which directly affect the lives of the people throughout the dominion.
The people of this country are becoming alarmed at government by order in council. They are losing patience with controls and regulations. They are becoming fed up with "bureaucracy, and they have good reason to be.
The hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) has given instances of how some orders in council have overridden the fundamental rights of the people of Canada by depriving them of the rlgnt to counsel when investigations are being carried on by officers of the crown.*
He has rendered a service to the dominion by bringing those orders, in council into the light of day; he has rendered a service to freedom and to justice in bringing them to the attention of the house and the country, and yet by this bill we are asked to approve all orders in council which have been, passed under the War Measures Act. Under section 2, subsection 3 of the bill, we have no right to look into those orders in council or to have them annulled, as is provided for other orders in council.
There are always some people about, and present company is not altogether excepted, who hold the view that the underlying principles of British justice and of our constitution are very fine principles indeed, so long as they do not interfere with their plans or activities, or prevent them from taking short-cuts to achieve the ends they have in view. No matter how good their intentions may be or how earnest they may be in their endeavours, such persons are a menace to the state if they have the power to override those principles.

National Emergency
A chief justice of England once said that "high capacity and ardent zeal never need to be more carefully watched than when they appear to have entered with all their might upon a wrong course."
In this connection I am reminded of a letter that Lord Disraeli, when Prime Minister of Great Britain, wrote to Queen Victoria who wanted a certain gentleman appointed Archbishop of Canterbury. He said:	"The Bishop of London sympathizes
with everything that is earnest, but what is earnest is not always true. On the contrary, error is often more earnest, than true."
It seems to me, sir, that the government of the dominion, in bringing this bill into the house, has proceeded upon a wrong course, very earnestly and no doubt very sincerely, but on a course that violates constitutional principles and, I may add, the principles of British justice.
I propose . to give one or two illustrations that have come to my notice to show how government orders and regulations affect men's lives, interfere with their means of livelihood and violate their fundamental rights.
Early this year a young man showed me a letter he had received from a government department. He was a carpenter in a very small way, and in 1942 had taken a contract to construct some small buildings, an undertaking with which he was not very familiar. Neither was he familiar with government regulations, but he made an honest effort to comply with them. When he paid the men who worked for him he deducted the tax from their wages, as required. A year or so after he had finished the contract, government officials inspected his books and sent him the letter to which I have just referred. In that letter he was informed that he was short about S10 of the amount he should have deducted from his workmen for taxes in 1942, and about $60 short of the amount he should have deducted in 1943. The letter went on to say in effect that, as he was just getting started in business and was not familiar with the regulations he would be fined only $25.
What is British justice coming to when a thing like that can happen in this country? Do hon. members realize what it means? It is a fundamental principle of law, which is subject to some exceptions, that a man is not guilty of a crime if he commits an innocent mistake. But the most shocking feature of the case is that under these regulations, government officials have the right to act as complainant, prosecutor, judge and jury, and impose a fine on a man without giving him an opportunity to be heard.
I say that this kind of thing must stop if we are to remain a free people.
Let me give another example, this time under selective service. A man who was a vulcanizer by trade had been ill fcfr about six months. When he was well enough to go to work he looked about for a job and found a vulcanizing firm in the city in which he lived, engaged in essential war work, which required his services. He knew the boss of this plant and wanted to work for him. He went to the selective service office, told them he was a vulcanizer and said he would like to work for this particular firm which required his services. Selective service officers, after looking through their cards, ordered him to go to work with another vulcanizing firm. He said he wanted to work with the man he knew, and an argument ensued. He noticed the card stated that the wages would be $140 a month, but he was told the wages would be $120 a month. This led to another argument, but in the end he was forced to go where he was ordered.	.
It is only natural that he did not go in a very good state of mind, and it followed that he and his boss did not get along very well. Finally he said to the boss, "This is not fair to you and it is not fair to me," and the boss who was fed up with him by this time, no doubt for very good reasons, called up selective service who said to send the man in. Before he went, however, a discharge card had to be filled out. Under the heading, "Reason for release" the boss wrote the words, "Claims to be sick," and this card was signed by both employer and employee.
When the workman went back to the selective service office with this card, though there was a shortage of vulcanizers in the town he was ordered to go to work for a certain company as a carpenter. He said that he was not a carpenter; that he had done carpentering work at one time but had sold his tools years ago, and that he was a vulcanizer. He was told, "Well, you can either go to work as a carpenter or you can go to work as a labourer."
Apparently selective service officials thought they had the right to punish him because he had the effrontery to speak up for himself in the belief that he had some rights as a Canadian citizen.
When he came to look at the card he had brought to the office, which both he and his employer had signed, he found that some official there had scratched out the words "Claims to be sick" and had written in their place "Unreliable." This, of course, was an out-and-out forgeYy and could not be justified on any grounds whatever.
National Emergency

This story gives us an example of how men are treated when they are governed by bureaucracy established through government orders in council and government regulations, and I %ay it must stop.
Now let me give another example of the way in which bureaucracy is carried on under national selective service. A man who conducted a restaurant business and rendered service to men engaged in heavy work by providing them with substantial meals had difficulty in obtaining waitresses. Selective service could not supply them. On one occasion after a long search he engaged a girl and drove her to the selective service office to have the necessary forms completed. When she came out of the office and got into his car he looked at her card and found that she had been directed to go to work for another restaurant.
Now let me give an example of a different kind. A man who had a service station and repair shop on the outskirts of a city went into the used car business in a small way in 1941. Last year he was notified that he must get a permit from the government to carry on a used car business. He filled out the form and received a permit.
This year he applied again to the government authorities for a permit, and received a letter in reply informing him that his application was refused on the ground that he had not adequate facilities to deal in second-hand cars. He had a service station, a repair garage and a good-sized lot adjoining it on which to park cars, but evidently this was not sufficient for some reason or another and a licence was refused. Not only was it refused, but he was ordered to sell the cars he had on hand and report to the government department when the sales had been made.
These are only a few instances that have come to my notice. I could cite many others, and no doubt many hon. members could cite a great many more of how affairs in this country are being carried on under government orders in council and government regulations rather than by acts of parliament.
In conclusion, may I quote again from Lord Hewart, who said:
Writers on the constitution have for a long time taught that its two leading features are the sovereignty of parliament and the rule of law. To tamper with one of them was, it might be thought, a sufficiently serious undertaking. But how more attractive to the ingenious and adventurous mind to employ the one to defeat the other, and to establish despotism on the ruins of both.
The government by this bill is attempting to defeat the functions of parliament and the
[Mr. Hazen.l
rule of law and by means of orders in council and regulations to establish a new despotism in time of peace.
The great national emergency that exists in Canada to-day is the attempt that the government is making to maintain a dictatorship now that the war is over.

Mr. Speaker, I hesitate to enter into this learned discussion on controls; but as a member since the beginning of the war of the government which has been administering the affairs of Canada, possibly I should reply to some of the statements which have been made in the discussion up to this time, more particularly those which were made this afternoon by the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett). Before doing so, I should like to say that I do not think there is anyone in this House of Commons or in Canada who is more opposed to controls of any kind than . I. Liberalism has always taught me to have objection to controls in so far as they are not necessary to preserve the rights of others. Naturally those of us who have been brought up in that belief have objection to the infliction of controls of any kind upon the people of the country to which we belong which are not absolutely necessary to the welfare of all of us.
But I think those of us who have had the privilege, unfortunate or otherwise, to have lived in this generation, we have all learned through the experience of time. We certainly have had an opportunity, equal to that of any generation that has ever lived, to understand the necessity for controls at a time when our nation is being attacked by the enemy. On two occasions within the lifetime of those of us who are gathered here democratic countries have found it necessary to defend democratic institutions. On each occasion that we have found it necessary to do so, it has been natural that we have had to utilize instruments in which we did not personally believe.
Anyone who believes in the freedom of democracy does not believe in war. But anyone who believes in the freedom of democracy knows that when democracy is attacked by those who believe in force, there is only one way in which that force can be effectively met, and that is by force. We all realize, too, that when we are placed in the position where we must of necessity use force, we must use instruments which are not the common instruments of a nation which is free. So that under those circumstances we have control.
I object to those who consider themselves radicals, who looking at the effectiveness of controls during war time advocate their main-

National Emergency
tenance during a time of peace. My reason for opposing that is very much the same reason as was given expression to a few moments ago by the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Hazen); my reason for opposing that is the same reason as was given this afternoon by the hon. member for Stan-stead, namely, that if the application of controls is continued long enough we shall be afflicted by the same kind of totalitarian state and totalitarian institutions against which we are compelled to fight when we defend democracy against those_ totalitarian institutions. I am as anxious as any one in this house to get rid of controls. I am sure I have in agreement with me, not only every member of the government but every member who sits on this side of the house. We always have wished to get rid of controls.
After having made that statement, I should like to say that there is a middle course between wishing to rid ourselves of controls overnight, and' wishing to maintain those controls for an exceptionally long period of time which may eventually land this country in a position where we would be threatened with a totalitarian form of government. That middle course is not necessarily expressed by Liberals, nor is it necessarily expressed by those who would take the course of totalitarianism. However, it is often expressed by people by whom we would least expect it to be expressed; it is expressed by businessmen; it is expressed by the people on the street; it is expressed by the leaders of finance. I should like to quote to the house an expression of opinion, given by one with whom many of us on this side of the house do not always agree, one with whom some hon. members on the other side of house never agree. Mr. Spinney of the bank of Montreal is reported in the Montreal Daily Star of December 3, 1945, as follows:
At the same time, Mr. Spinney said, there must be a realization that for many months to come there still would be a need for some of the controls introduced during the war years.
"It is quite evident that inflationary pressures are now, if anything, more intense and more fraught with potential danger than at any time during the years of actual conflict.
In consequence, the need for continuance of the war-time pattern of voluntary restraint, and for intelligent acceptance of appropriate stabilization controls still remains as a challenge to $he good sense of the Canadian people.
The manner in which we meet that challenge will determine whether we tackle the tasks of reconstruction against a background of stable monetary conditions or in the turbulent atmosphere of inflationary boom and subsequent collapse.
With that statement which appears in the press of yesterday I think most members of the house will agree, particularly the latter part of it which says that if we took off overnight all controls at the end of a war such as we have just passed through, the result would be the subsequent collapse of our institutions. All one needs to do to be persuaded of that is to read the history of the period immediately following the last war, when countries which followed that course brought upon themselves great difficulties from which they had greater difficulty in extricating themselves. With that statement of the president of the bank of Montreal before us together with the experience of other countries following the last war, may I now refer to some of the remarks that were made this afternoon?
The hon. member for Stanstead took the position that this bill was most confusing, and in order to prove his point he read from the preamble of the bill to show that it was most confusing. I should like to read part of the preamble to the bill, and I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the intention of the government could not be set out more plainly than it appears in the preamble. The preamble says:
And whereas the national emergency .arising out of the war has continued since the unconditional surrender of Germany and Japan and is still continuing; and whereas it is essential in the national interest that certain transitional powers continue to be exercisable by the governor in council during the continuation of the exceptional conditions brought about by the war and it is preferable that such transitional powers be exercised hereafter under special authority in that behalf conferred by parliament instead of being exercised under the War Measures Act; -and whereas in the existing circumstances it is essential that certain acts and things done and authorized and certain orders and regulations1 made under the War Measures Act be continued in force and that the governor in council be authorized to do and authorize such further acts .and things and make such further orders and regulations as he may deem necessary or advisable by Teason of the emergency .and for the purpose of the discontinuance, in an orderly manner .as the emergency permits, of measures adopted during and by reason of the emergency: Therefore His Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the .Senate and House of 'Commons of Canada, enacts as follows
That language seems to me to be perfectly plain; there is no confusion in it at all.

That, of course, is the bill which is to be submitted to the committee for consideration. That is the bill I am speaking to. For bill No. 15 which was before the house, another bill is being substituted which expresses very clearly the position. May I say that I am only replying to the hon. member for Stanstead, who this afternoon read part of the preamble from the original bill and part of the preamble from the second bill and indicated that the preamble of the second bill was confusing. I am simply reading from the preamble of the second bill to indicate that it is not confusing; that it is perfectly plain.
In the speeches to which I have just listened the statement has been made over and over again that we are asking the members of this house to permit the government to pass legislation over which this parliament will have no control. The members who make that statement have not read the bill. The bill definitely says that what we are doing is just what the preamble outlines, namely, asking the house to permit the government to continue in existence the orders in council which were passed during the war and which it is necessary to have continued for a few months after the war. The bill goes on to provide that within a certain period of time the government must place on the table of the house any order that it passes and, further, that either the House of Commons or the Senate can take action to make that particular order inoperative. There is nothing in the bill which says that but for more than a few days the government has authority to legislate without that legislation having been given consideration by the membership of the house and the senate as well, and the bill contains the further extraordinary provision, one that I never heard of before in any bill, that in order to protect the rights of the members of this house and of the members of the senate, either house may prevent such an order from becoming the law of this country. With such a provision in the bill I cannot understand why all this discussion is taking place at this time. It must be because certain members of the opposition have in their minds ideas which I am sure are not in the minds of the great mass of the people of this country, and in order to make plain what the hon. member for Stanstead did have in his mind this afternoon, I should -like to read some of the statements he made, bringing them a little closer together than they appear in the long.legal argument that he put before the house.

In the first place I read this:
If I grasp the significance of the terminology, it means that there was an emergency, that there is not an emergency now, but to retreat from the emergency we must have emergency powers. That is what I believe the hill means.
Well, Mr. Speaker, if anything could be more confusing than that particular statement except confusion itself I do not know what it is. After having read part of the preamble into the records of this house the hon. member immediately proceeded to state that this part of the preamble means exactly the opposite of what it does mean. Then he went on to say:
If there he an emergency, it is not a war emergency. If there be an emergency, it is an emergency which arises from the totalitarian legislation which we enacted to fight and defeat a totalitarian people.
Well, Mr. Speaker, if it was legislation enacted to. fight and defeat a totalitarian people, surely it is legislation which has arisen out of the war to cover emergency acts of this government done for the very purpose of assisting in fighting and defeating a totalitarian people; and this legislation arises out of the fact that we have been at war and that there are continuing results from that
war.	He goes on to say:
I do not criticize those who had the responsibility of enacting the legislation that brought these controls -about. They were anxious to win the war. They had but one aim in view, and they have achieved that aim. But to achieve it they paid a price.
Mr. Speaker, I do not look for any higher eulogy of the government of the Dominion of Canada which carried on during the war than that which was made by the hon. member for Stanstead in his criticism of the government. Let me read it again:
I do not criticize those who had the responsibility of enacting the legislation that brought these controls about. They were anxious to win the war. They had but one aim in view and they have -achieved that -aim.
But to achieve it they paid the price.
Yes, Mr. Speaker. Not the members of the government paid the price, particularly. The people of the Dominion of Canada paid the price. The people of all the democratic nations of the world fighting against the totalitarian form of government paid the price, but I do not know that I am in agreement with the hon. member for Stanstead in all that he said in regard to what that price
was.	He does go on to say this:
When we come to consider our present situation and determine what course we should follow, we cannot hope to get back to normal without going through some turbulence, without experiencing some inconvenience. Anybody

National Emergency
who takes a stimulant, anybody who develops artificial energy within himself must pay a price, and Canada just cannot afford to taper off in a matter of this kind.
May I call attention to the fact that my hon. friend believes that we cannot get away from this war without turbulence. We, the members of the government, believe that by acting sensibly we can get away from this war, in Canada, without turbulence, and we intend to try so to conduct the affairs of Canada, in getting ourselves from the war into a period of established peace, that turbulence will not be necessary within the dominion. Of course I think he is correct when he says that we cannot get away from it without experiencing some inconvenience; and this inconvenience the people of Canada are prepared to meet, even the inconvenience of the continuation of those controls which are necessary to bridge us over from the period of war into the period of peace. The hon. member goes on to say:
I submit that the emergency which confronts Canada to-day is not a war emergency; it is an emergency which arises out of the legislation which we enacted to win the war. We cannot ease ourselves out of it, because that is impossible.
The inference from that is that we should go out with one jump. We must not ease ourselves out; we must take one leap right out of the war and into peace, and in doing so avoid the necessity of having legislation of this kind. That not only would be most ridiculous, but would have an effect upon the people of this country such as nothing which has been done up to date, either by the government or by any of those who are attempting to hinder what is being done by the government, to bring turbulence; it would have an effect more detrimental to the people of this country than anything else which I can conceive of. He says:
Somebody has threatened us with terrible trouble, with great evils, unless these controls be continued. What are these great perils? The hon. member . . . tells us that flour went up, that sugar went up in price

Mr. Speaker, I shall not attempt to answer in detail the speech made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). He spent his whole time in discussing nerves and controls. His whole speech demonstrated nerve without control. It was amazing to sit and listen to the speech of the spokesman of the government in power in which he tried to illustrate to the house the necessity of controls and nerves without attempting to portray the role of members of parliament in the situation.
In his opening speech on Bill No. 15 in its original form the Minister of Justice (Mr. St, Laurent) pointed to two main questions before the- house. He said that this bill required two distinct things, a declaration of a post-war emergency and the delegation of the powers of parliament to the government of

Canada. There is nobody in Canada who does not realize that in war time stringent controls are necessary in many aspects of human life. Nobody will disagree with the government when they say in the bill, as amended, that the war-time condition will stop on the first day of January, 1946. We all agree with the government when they say that because of war our social, economic, trade and home conditions have been upset. We all agree with certain measures which the government brought in during the war. By this bill the government seeks to extend and increase them to meet a different emergency in post-war days. The emergency we have now is not that of war entirely; it is the coo-[DOT] sequence of our war-time economy and a consequence of the present government's wartime controls, by order in council and administrative regulations.
After listening to the speech made by the minister to-night, in which he emphasized his viewpoint and, I believe, the viewpoint of the government, one would almost be compelled to come to the conclusion that there was nobody but Hitler who could govern. There is nobody but the little autocrat who spoke to-night who has sole power and who wants to increase that power, who can better exemplify the autocracy he wants to extend.

speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: BILL TO CONFER CERTAIN POWERS UPON THE GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
No explanation of mine could be better than the demonstration already given by the previous speaker.
The War Measures Act, which was passed at the beginning of the war, declared that because a state of war existed certain powers must be vested in parliament and that parliament must delegate certain of those powers to the government. Then we find that the government has delegated to the executive of the government, the cabinet, the privy council, the right to carry on by order in council the hitherto unknown and undemocratic policy of legislating to the extent of abrogating statutes and interfering with civil and property rights, of interfering with the privilege of carrying on your trade, of marketing your own produce, of living your own life as you might see it. I agree that to an extent many of those policies were necessary. We now find that after the war is over, so far as combat is concerned, the government are coming back to parliament and telling us that they are going to declare it over within a few short days and asking us to approve everything the order in council government did up to that date and to grant them the power to extend their regulations. In other words, it definitely illustrates, as did the minister's

National Emergency
speech to-night, the total forgetfulness of this government or of the cabinet of the government of any legislating power in Canada other than the King cabinet. I hope that all hon. members do not agree with this. The government is forgetful of the fact that there are provincial legislatures and municipal institutions which can take the burden off this government of displacing the war-tom economy of Canada and of helping it to restore peace-time conditions. The minister did not refer to that; it did not occur to him that anybody but a little secret council, a little cabinet, an executive committee, could handle the situation which the law and the constitution of the country requires to be handled by other than the parliament of Canada, except in an emergency.
I say to him and to hon. members that certain controls are necessary. During war time, and because of a war economy, government action must be centred more in the federal parliament than in peace time, and to a degree parliament must place more confidence ' and more power in the executive or the privy council.
As Mark Antony said, Caesar was ambitious when he tried to turn autocracy into tyranny and lost his life. He illustrated for all time the lust of those in power for greater power, and the unwillingness of those with power to surrender that power. That has been further demonstrated not only by this bill, not only by this cabinet but, to the umpteenth degree, by the remarks of the minister who preceded me.
What does this bill do? For a while I thought we were to speak only on the original bill, that bill No. 2 was only a suggestion as to what the government might do at a future date if we gave our blessing to bill No. 1. However, the minister took the liberty to discuss bill No. 2, and emphasized the wording of the preamble where in three or four places it stated that the situation to-day required certain transitional powers to be given by parliament to the executive, that it asked that certain things should be done and that certain orders and regulations under the War Measures Act should be continued. The bill contains very little that is certain. Let me read the powers which are sought:
(a)	providing for and maintaining the armed forces of Canada during the occupation of enemy territory and demobilization and providing for the rehabilitation of members thereof . . .
Power to do every bit of that, with the possible exception of some rehabilitation measures, is already in the hands of the cabinet; but as far as the army is concerned, how could they ask for more outright and absolute power? Then the next paragraph states:
(b)	facilitating the readjustment of industry and commerce to the requirements of the community in time of peace . . .
To what community, may I ask? Is it the community of the hon. gentleman who just spoke, the Minister of Agriculture, or is it some other little community within our country? Is it the community of the cabinet, as someone suggests? Perhaps that is the meaning we should take from it. They want power to facilitate the readjustment of industry and commerce to the requirements of the community in time of peace. Perhaps it is the world community. What does that not cover? It covers anything the government-not the government, but the executive committee of the government-may hereafter think will tend to facilitate the readjustment of the war-torn world. Could one get any broader power than that? Then the next clause goes on:
(c)	maintaining, controlling and regulating supplies and services, prices, transportation, use and occupation of property-
They should have put "real and personal" there, so that we would know there was no property they could not control.
-rentals, employment, or salaries and wages
I wonder why they did not include the control of going to church. That is about the only thing I can think of that they have omitted.	.
(d)	assisting the relief of suffering and the restoration and distribution of essential supplies and services in any part of His Majesty's dominions or in foreign countries that are in grave distress as the result of the war . . .
Does that not mean every place where distress may exist, in the minds of the executive committee of this house? Then:
(e)	continuing and discontinuing in an orderly manner, as the- emergency permits-
It does not say as the war emergency permits, but any emergency.
-measures adopted during and by reason of the war.
The first bill No. 15 had something that was specific, something that was certain; but in the second bill No. 15 the only certainty was the word "certain" used in the preamble. Does this bill represent the government's intention to^give back the powers which under the constitution heretofore belonged to the parliament of Canada. It does not purport to give any powers to parliament but gives them directly to the executive committee. It is a case of all power to the privy council and no power to parliament. Does it favour the legislatures of our provinces reassuming any of their pre-war privileges and obligations? It does not. It seems to represent the
National Emergency

very opposite. Does it diminish the powers of the nomelective boards and commissions? No. This bill as now drafted wants the parliament of Canada, the legislatures of Canada, the municipal councils of Canada, the people of Canada, the government of the day and all members of this house to delegate to the cabinet not only the power to legislate but the power to delegate to other men and other boards, who have never been elected by the exercise of any franchise, power to abrogate statutes and make orders arid regulations having the force of law. That is not democracy. I say that the time has come when, parliament should not delegate any powers it has to men who have not been appointed to their positions by the democratic franchise. To me that is the important thing about this bill. It does not by any means limit, curtail or show any desire to stop the order in council government that has been so obnoxious to the Canadian people. Under the amended bill the powers are so general and so all-inclusive that I cannot conceive of anjThing being more all-embracing. Surely we in Canada, having beaten the totalitarian states, must work against totalitarianism within our own state. The people now desire to see a return to pre-war privileges, to peace-time prosperity and happiness, to the privileges of British and Canadian citizenship and freedom, to the use of their property without having the government take control of all property rights, without submitting its orders even to the members of the House of Commons until long after they have been passed.
The minister said that ample provision is made for these orders in council to be tabled in the house and for hon. members to pass upon them. I ask hon. gentlemen how practical it is to place a resolution on the order paper and have it discussed, with the government taking precedence for its business as it has for the last five years. How will that be worked out? I do not want to go through all the provisions of the bill in detail, but let us see when it may be terminated. Section 6 of the amended bill states:
Subject as hereinafter provided, this act shall expire on the thirty-first day of December, one thousand nine hundred and forty-six, if parliament meets during November or December, one thousand nine hundred and forty-six-
The Prime Minister or the cabinet, who heretofore have not called parliament to meet to sanction their orders in council, are not likely to change their ways and call a meeting of parliament next November or December for the sole purpose of submitting to the members of the House of Commons the

products of their imagination and those of their dollar-a-year men, unless they have a complete change of policy. But it goes on: -but if parliament does not so meet it shall expire on the fifteenth day after parliament first meets during the year one thousand nine hundred and forty-seven-
It does not say when it will meet, because it may be postponed until the next fall. We have been running a year late now in our parliamentary sessions, so that we do not know whether it will be called until November or December, 194S. The section continues:

provided that, if at any time while this act is in force, addresses are presented to the governor general by the Senate and House of Commons respectively, praying that this act should be continued in force for a further period, not in any case exceeding one year, from the time at which it would otherwise expire and the governor in council so orders, this act shall continue in force for that further period.
As the Minister of Agriculture has shown so well to-night, we can well imagine a continuation of order in council government without even the possibility of calling parliament to let members have an opportunity of seeing these matters, whether the government ever lets them come to a discussion or not. Under those circumstances we have to look at this bill, not as a declaration of the necessity of controls, but as a declaration iby the cabinet of contempt for parliament, of contempt for the legislators, of contempt for democracy and of contempt for the people. I see nothing in it to indicate in any way any desire, hope, wish or possibility of returning to the democratic and freedom loving people of Canada privilege of having their elected representatives make and sustain their own laws.

Mr. Speaker, I think at this stage of the debate it is necessary to pause and take stock of this situation. We have had presented to us bill No. 15, the original bill, by which we had understood until a few moments ago that we were bound and circumscribed in this debate. Then, after certain significant events of recent days we have had held out an enticing bit of bait in the form of a revised bill. Notwithstanding what the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) said a few minutes ago, the bill before the house at the moment is the original bill No. 15 and when this house votes on the second reading it is voting for the second reading of the original bill. In the meantime the government is holding out a little bit beyond our grasp this bait in the form of a revised bill which cannot be put before this house until we are in committee of the whole. There is the issue before this house on the second reading of the Original bill No.

National Emergency
15. What is the principle of that bill? I say that the principle of that bill is such that no self-respecting parliament in this month of December, 1945, could possibly consider it. There has been introduced a bit of windowdressing, a bit of bait, but .parliament is faced with the stark reality of bill No. 15.
Since this bill was first introduced and since this debate first began a week ago last Friday, several mysteries about it have perhaps been cleared up. But one mystery has not been cleared up. The veil of secrecy still enshrouds the author of the bill. The hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), in his masterly address in this chamber a week ago last Friday challenged the government to declare who was the author and draftsman of this bill. That challenge has not been met and secrecy still surrounds the authorship of the bill. But if one will look for a moment at the substitute bill which is being dangled just out of the grasp of this chamber, he will perhaps see a familiar hand in the authorship and draftsmanship, a hand -which apparently was not present in this country when the original bill No. 15 was drafted.
Let us face certain simple facts which I fear have been lost sight of somewhat, certainly in the speech to-night by the Minister of Agriculture. In passing, I wish to pay the Minister of Agriculture a compliment. When the government get deep into a hole they always call upon the Minister of Agriculture to pull them out. We need no further proof of the fact that in this debate the government are in a hole, a deep hole, than the fact that they have called upon the Minister of Agriculture to come to the rescue.
It has been said that the constitutional position is such that in a time of national peril the authority to enact extraordinary measures to meet extraordinary situations is vested -in the governor in council. Of course that is absolute nonsense. All that the privy council has ever said is that in times of great national emergency, where the whole nation is in dire peril, the classes of subjects enumerated in sections 91 and 92 of the British North America Act take on new aspects. Under the peace, order and good government clause extraordinary powers are vested, not in the governor in council but in parliament, to take the measures required to ipeet such situations.
Those powers rest, not in the governor in council but in the members of parliament, the elected representatives of the people. Are we to discharge our responsibility at this time by saying, "Well, we are content to go on and adopt what the nineteenth parliament did in 47696-186
time of war, even though we have now come to a time of peace." That is the responsibility which faces this house at the present time.
Section 5 of this bill means this: The government is seeking to get out from under its responsibility, the responsibility for that teeming mass of orders in council and treasury minutes which now number close to 100,000. The government is asking this parliament to adopt a whole mass of orders in council and treasury minutes, in many cases sight unseen. Are we, the twentieth parliament, elected in a time of peace, elected to restore parliament to its proper function, prepared now to abdicate so completely that we not only transfer to the governor in council the powers that we possess but assume the whole load of responsibility for everything the government has done by order in council, by regulation and by treasury minute since the War Measures Act came into effect in September, 1939?
Can any self-respecting parliament in December, 1945, take on that responsibility? I say it cannot.
In the three months that I have sat in this chamber I have been impressed with the care which has been exercised on many occasions in scrutinizing the particular form of the legislation placed before the house and the committees. That is most commendable; that is parliament doing its duty. It should scrutinize every letter and- word placed before it in the form of bills and resolutions. But what does this government ask of us? It asks that without so much as seeing the contents of many of these orders in council we simply adopt them and take full responsibility for them. In time to come, when we find out what we have done in our folly they will say to us, "Oh, that is not our act, you took that over; you took the responsibility and it is your responsibility, the responsibility of the twentieth parliament of Canada."
There is no escape from that position. Does the new bill make any improvement in that respect? It does not. Look at section 2, subsection 1 (e) and section 4 of this bill, and you will see that the position under the new bill is precisely the same as the position under the original bill. Parliament is asked to accept all responsibility for what has been going on in this country since September, 1939, by order in council, by government regulation and by treasury minute. I see no improvement in the new bill in that regard.
I say further that the effect of section 3 of the bill is that parliament abdicates, and abdicates completely, its functions. It does not matter apparently that peace has come. No; the war complex still remains with the

National Emergency

government because with the war goes power, and that is the complex of the government which has conceived and presented this bill to parliament.
Let no one be misled by the provision requiring tabling of the orders in council. The old bill, by section 3, subsection 4, provided for the tabling of orders in council as soon as might be. Section 4 of the new bill expands that provision to some extent. But what is the situation in fact? Suppose the orders in council are tabled-not the old orders in council because there is no obligation on the government under either of these bills that the governor in council shall table the old orders in council. Not one of those orders does the governor in council have to table, only orders passed in the future. Then the government tells you that if parliament does not like these orders, parliament can annul them; but what is involved in that? It means that a private member's resolution must be presented and carried through both houses of parliament. If there is one thing that all the new members of parliament have learned it is this, that private members' resolutions have no hope whatever of getting to a vote. How many private members' resolutions have come to a vote this session, although we spent many days and evenings in discussing them? Only one, and that because it apparently happened to suit the government. There is no safeguard whatsoever of the rights of parliament in that provision.
Some hon. members on the other side of the house speak as though this were the only legislature in the land. It is a convenient view for the government to take. As a matter of fact, if the government goes on pursuing the course which it has pursued since September, 1939, this parliament will become in fact the only legislature in Canada, because the rights of the provincial legislatures have been constantly trampled and trespassed upon by this government without regard to the rights of the provinces. There has been no indication whatever of a change of heart or a repentant attitude on the part of the government in this regard, and so we can go on expecting the same disregard of provincial rights. Our system of government is not a unitary system but a federal system. We have legislatures which are capable of assuming responsibility for property and civil rights in the provinces, and this government is not required to adopt extraordinary measures to meet problems which can be coped with by legislatures acting within the scope of their constitutional powers.
In the impassioned contribution which was made to this debate this evening by the Min-

ister of Agriculture, he put a glowing picture before us. I am paraphrasing the gist of his remarks. It may be, he said, that this bill gives the government extraordinary powers but, after all, you can trust us because we are not the kind of people to use extraordinary powers in an arbitrary way. Look at us, he said; we won the war.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that the government did not win the war. The boys who fought on the battlefields, the labourers working in the factories and munition plants, the farmers toiling in the fields, the people of Canada won the war. The government takes a great deal of credit for winning the war, credit which is not theirs.
Let us see what we can expect from this government. Can one find a better test of what one might expect in the exercise of the extraordinary powers the government is asking parliament to confer than to look at what the government has been doing under the powers conferred upon it by the War Measures Act? We do not need to go back very far, not farther than the 6th of September, 1945. 'What has been happening while parliament has been in session? I do not need to weary the house by an enumeration of the occasions upon which the government denied parliament essential information for which it asked. It became monotonous, these denials of information which parliament sought. We remember what happened about the Canadian information service. The government at one fell swoop, while parliament was in session, without consulting it at all, did away with the wartime information board and by order in council placed the appropriations which parliament had provided for the wartime information board at the disposal of the government's new creation, the Canadian information service, and when we asked for the minutes to be tabled we were told: "Oh, no; that is a privileged document. We cannot trust parliament with that information. Only the government is capable of treating that information as it ought to be treated."
''The last hon. member who spoke in this debate spoke truly when he said that this government has treated parliament with contempt. I go farther and say that it has treated parliament with studied contempt.
I refer to the situation with regard to appropriations. As long as government by order in council continues, parliament will be asked to vote blindly tremendous sums of money to be expended in any way the governor in council sees fit, without any effective restraint, restriction or control by parliament. We have put hundreds of millions of dollars at the disposal of the governor in council.

National Emergency
Have we had any proper accounting? Hon. members know that the money was spent before we were ever asked to vote it. You know, Mr. Speaker, that we were not. offered any details of the items of expenditure in the estimates. Frequently they were brought in with apologies. Are we to continue that situation in time of peace? It would be an abdication of the functions of parliament, and I say that no self-respecting parliament dare do such a thing.
We know perfectly well that as long as this bureaucratic system continues, the power is not exercised by hon. gentlemen sitting on the treasury benches opposite but by controllers. administering policies that daily affect the lives of all our people. Very often when we wanted to know what great policies were in the making we had to wait for some public pronouncement by one of these bureaucrats. We did not get it from the government; we did not get it in parliament. We had to wait until the bureaucrats announced it publicly.
Is that democracy? Never. In this new bill we have the very same thing. The governor in council may continue to legislate by order in council while parliament is still in session. That alone is enough to condemn the bill. Let every hon. member understand that if he votes for the second reading he is voting in support of legislation to provide that the governor in council may continue to legislate by order in council even while the representatives of the people are assembled in session in parliament.
The situation would not have been so bad as it is if, along with the power which the government has enjoyed, there had been a proper appreciation of and a rising to its responsibilities, but we have had a deplorable situation revealed in this house. Although all aspects of labour relations were vested in the federal government under the extraordinary powers conferred by the War Measures Act, when the Ford strike took place at Windsor the members of the house asked what this government was going to do about it, and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) rose in his place and said in 'effect: We wash our hands of this; it is not a matter for us because the responsibility rests on the provincial government. Although this government had deprived the provincial governments of jurisdiction in these matters, this government said that the responsibility still rested on the provinces even though the power was vested in the dominion. I say that was a denial of this government's responsibility even while they possessed the power.

We have not been offered in this debate what every member had a right to expect, and that was an undertaking by the government when they brought in this bill that they would bring in at the same time a programme for the demobilization of the bureaucracy with which this country has become enmeshed. We have not had laid before us a properly integrated or comprehensive programme of demobilization of controls. They have not told us what, if any, objectives they are aiming at in connection with doing away with these wartime controls. No; we have waited in vain for that, and apparently we are not to be told. Are we told that there is any hope of easing the pressure of ceilings on wages and salaries? No; we have not been told that. Has there been any indication of any attempt on the part of the government to eliminate the inequalities which have existed with respect to wages, where people engaged in civilian production have not been paid on a scale commensurate with that paid to people engaged in war-time production? No; there has been no word of that. Has any hope at all been held out for the salaried workers, the white-collared people upon whom these controls have rested so oppressively during the war? No. There is not one ray of hope in anything which has fallen from the mouth of a member of the government during this debate-not one word. It is an amazing exhibition of bankruptcy of policy and lack of vision on the part of this government.
