subtopic: BILL TO CONFER CERTAIN POWERS UPON THE GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext: They elected us too.

subtopic: BILL TO CONFER CERTAIN POWERS UPON THE GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
They expected something higher and better from us than to treat this issue with levity.
What is the significance of this bill? I have said that there is in section 3 a complete abdication by parliament. That is what is involved. We may prate about the supremacy of parliament; but if this bill passes, the so-called supremacy of parliament becomes nothing but a snare and a delusion, a shell and a sham. Parliament is invited by this measure to turn its supremacy into a sham, because real power will rest not with parliament but with the governor in council, and it will be based on the abdication by parliament of its proper constitutional function.
Something like three hundred years ago a man strode into the parliament hall at WesU
National Emergency

minster and, pointing to the mace which rested on the table, said, "Take away that bauble." The government of the day is not saying to this parliament, "Take away that bauble", but, "Hand that bauble over to us." we might as well see in fact that mace preceding a procession to the executive council chamber, because that is where the effective . legislative power of this country will rest if bill No. 15 is passed.
I said something about judging this government on its recent record. We do not need to go back very far to find enough wherewith to answer the question, "Can the leopard change its spots?" with an emphatic "no". I refer back to the twelfth day of November, when the then Acting Prime Minister dropped on this chamber an atomic bomb. His statement, which is to be found on page 2020 of Hansard, is unquestionably the most amazing which we shall have in this session. I daresay it will be many a year, and many a parliament will come and go in this country, before a more remarkable, a more astounding statement will be made in this chamber, certainly by a minister of the crown. There are two or three sentences of it which ought to be impressed by now indelibly on the minds of hon. members. The Acting Prime Minister said this:
There is danger that the House of Commons may be losing sight of its real functions, which are to vote supply, to control expenditure and to enact legislation.
Look at those three things: vote supply, control expenditure, enact legislation. Compare them with this bill, and what do we see? Voting of supply? _ Yes; voting in the dark. Certainly we can go on voting money in the dark. That is the situation to-day. Second, to control expenditure. Seriously, Mr. Speaker, what' effective control over expenditure exists so long as government by order in council can be continued, so long as they can go on spending the money in advance and come back to parliament later and ask parliament to vote the money, not to vote it according to proper estimates, but to vote it in the dark. "Trust the government"! Is parliament prepare^ to trust the government to the extent that it is ready to abdicate? I hope not. The third function is to enact legislation; and we as a parliament are asked non' to abdicate in favour of the governor in council this last of our remaining powers and responsibilities, the enactment of legislation. Yes; turn all these functions over to the government. And to a government with what conception of its relationship and re-

sponsibility to parliament? A government which measures its responsibility in these terms: Hansard, page 2020:
The authority of the government is not delegated by the House of Commons; the authority of the government is received from the crown.
I want to put alongside of that amazing statement a more orthodox statement. It is this:
It is impossible to imagine that the people of Canada will consent to pay the enormous sums which they are being called upon to provide by way of taxation . . . and will sit silent under the government's refusal to give them any information as to how their money has been spent.
That is the exact situation we have to-day, where we are not given information to which we are entitled. These last words I have quoted are those of the right hon. gentleman who is now Prime Minister of this country; they were uttered in this house in 1921, and reported in Hansard of that year, at page 1292.
What has already happened as a result of the introduction of this bill? I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that the whole cause of interprovincial cooperation, of cooperation between the dominion and the provinces, of constitutional reform, has been set back a long distance by the introduction of this bill, which plainly shows the hand of the government. It is a good thing that the provincial premiers met last week while parliament still had this bill before it. You know what happened. The voice of the provincial governments was heard speaking emphatically and unanimously in demanding that this bill be withdrawn, because inherent in it is the denial of the constitutional rights of the provinces. If this parliament should pass this bill it will have gone a long way toward rewriting the British North America Act to the infinite disadvantage of the provincial legislatures.
Another result which has followed the introduction of this bill in the house has been the most widespread expression of an outraged public opinion. That is one reason why the government to-day is holding out that bait in the form of a revised bill, which still is just beyond the grasp of parliament. I say to you that we are witnessing, in the step which the government has taken this week in dangling this new bill before us, an abject, even if a strategic, retreat on their part. There has Been no more complete vindication of the stand of an opposition at any time in the history of this land than has been seen in the vindication of the stand of the opposition on this bill since its attitude was shown in this chamber a week ago last Friday. We have seen the most widespread expressions of con-

National Emergency
demnation from all sections of the Canadian public, a denunciation of the arbitrary measures and arbitrary intent on the part of this government; and if I may say so, I feel sorry for hon. members opposite, who were put in the humiliating position of having to choose between support of the government and the course which they know they ought to follow on this bill; that is, the putting aside of arbitrary measures.
Many hon. members opposite have taken a firm public stand on many an occasion against any trespass upon the rights of the provincial legislatures. But here, without so much as consulting the provincial legislatures, the government has undertaken to trample upon and ride roughshod over the sacred constitutional rights of these legislatures. It is interesting to note that the public has rebuked the government. It is not only the opposition that has rebuked the government but the public. The provincial premiers have rebuked the government, and now the government appears to be accepting the rebuke. At least it. would have us think so.
Let the government learn its lesson out of this: That this parliament has no intention of abdicating its functions in favour of an arbitrary government. Look-at these bills. Time does not permit an exhaustive analysis, but I say that every power the government sought under the original bill it has under the new bill, and those vaunted safeguards that the Minister of Agriculture boasted about to-night do not amount to a snap of the fingers. Those safeguards are a sham. They are a snare and a delusion.
I said at the outset that we have to face the question whether in this approaching vote we as a House of Commons will give support to the principle of the bill. The principal of the bill is the abdication of the functions of parliament in favour of a cabinet which shows it does not regard itself as responsible to parliament. That is the principle of the bill. The principle of the bill is the right to go on legislating by order in council while parliament is in session, the right to prevent parliament. from having any effective means of bringing those orders in council under review even when we are called into session. Here we are told that the emergency is so great that we cannot wait until the next session of parliament, a scant two and a half months away, and that the government must have all these powers they had under the War Measures Act, and the powers sought under the original bill No. 15. The government has shown its hand, a greedy hand, reaching out for power. The complex that has dominated
this government in time of war dominates it to-day. That is the principle of the bill and there is no escape from it.
Is parliament going to permit itself to be reduced to a rubber stamp? I offer this quotation to the house, and I give it as precisely fitting the situation that is facing this country to-day.
. . . the government has proceeded, in practically everything it has done, as if it were .an executive wholly independent of the House of Commens, rather than an executive which derives its powers from and is responsible to the House of Commons. Indeed, the House of Commons has come to be, in the phrase used by the Prime Minister himself not so long ago, a sort of rubber- stamp for what the ministry may choose to do, regardless of how its own wishes and desires may be expressed, and regardless of how much those wishes and desires may represent the wishes and desires of the people at large.
That quotation is taken from a speech delivered in this house by the present Prime Minister and is to be found in Hansard of 1934, at page 42.
If the government really meant to show a change of heart in that phantom bill which is not before us yet officially, but which is dangled before us, what course would they have followed? Certainly not the course they have actually followed. The course they would have followed, the manly course, would have been to come to the house and say, "We wish to withdraw this bill; we made a blunder, we frankly confess it; we know we have outraged public opinion and are in the wrong and therefore we wish to withdraw this bill and introduce a new one." That is what they ought to have done but it is what they did not do. They would have brought before us a comprehensive programme for the demobilization of this bureaucracy that oppresses us. They would have shown us the objects at which they should be aiming and toward which they should be bending every effort.. But they did not do that. They had not the courage to do it.

As I was saying, the criticism was directed toward something that took place in 1931, when a measure of control was sought to be introduced into this country under new circumstances, when we had a depression such as the world has never seen before.
That brings up the question of the attitude of this group, and I am talking of the group that is in this house to-day. The Progressive Conservative party in this house represents the Progressive Conservative party in Canada to-day and I should like to define to some extent our stand on this matter of control.
It has been said several times in this house that we agree that a certain amount of control is necessary for the orderly transition from war-time to peace-time conditions. That was said by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) when the war expenditures appropriation came up at the beginning of the session. It was said by myself on that occasion. It has been said in the past-not in the dim and distant past but in the spring of this year-by the leader of this party. It was said again a week ago last Friday by the hon. member for Lake Centre. That is our position, and we have no hesitation in avowing it. We realize that a certain measure of control is necessary for the orderly transition from war-time to peace-time economy. That, then, is what we believe with regard to the principle of control; that only a limited control is necessary, and that it should be maintained only for the period of the emergency. There is no inconsistency as between our belief and our stand on this bill.
While we believe in the principle of that ' limited control for that limited period, wTe also believe in those principles of our constitution which guarantee to the subject his full liberty and the preseryation of his initiative and enterprise. Because we. believe in the principles of our constitution; because we believe that this bill infringes those principles; because it infringes the liberty of the subject in an unwarranted and unjustified and unnecessary manner, we oppose this bill.
This bill should have 'been a new one, not, as the hon. member for Eglinton has said, a sort of bait dangled just out of our reach.
I am glad to find that the leader of the C.C.F. is in agreement on that point. I do not just know where we stand here, whether this is a new draft of a proposed bill or whether we should be discussing the original bill. However, let us say that we are considering the new bill which will be submitted when we get into committee. It still goes too far. It attempts to grant powers which are unnecessary to cope with the emergency, but chiefly it is objectionable because it seeks to grant in the transitional peace-time period powers which were sought and used for war purposes. That is what we object to. We have it from the government's own statement that the powers which they needed during the war are not necessary in peace. They cannot understand why we criticize them for seeking to extend those powers.
In this connection I should like to refer to the speech made in this house this evening by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). While the minister was making his speech, I could not help thinking that he

should have been a lawyer, and I was not surprised to hear him say during the course of his remarks that at one time he had studied for the _ law. At the commencement of his remarks he outlined his absolute detestation of controls; he said that he could not get rid of them too quickly, and then we heard him say in his speech that he was a pretty good controller. As I listened to him announce his detestation of controls, I was reminded of a story which attaches to a famous lawyer.
When confronted with a troublesome piece of evidence a friend-said to this lawyer, "You cannot use that piece of evidence on appeal because it will destroy your case if you mention it.." This famous lawyer replied, "No; that will not be any trouble. I will read the evidence through once; I will repeat it again with comments on each sentence; I will repeat it again the third) time and contrast it with the evidence on the other side. Then, when my learned friend gets up to deal with his case the court will say to him, 'Oh, we have heard enough about that; we cannot be bothered to go into it.' " As the minister dealt with the extent of his detestation of control, I could not avoid being reminded of that story.
Hon. members will recall that not much later in his speech the minister proceeded to tell us just how much had been accomplished by controls, just how good the controls were and how good he was as a controller. He told us of the avalanche of hogs he had finally sent over to England, or something like that. There is really no doubt as to the attitude of mind of the ministers who sit on the government benches. They like controls. They have done what they regard1 as a good job by means of controls and they are reluctant to part with them now in time of peace.
We detest controls as much as the minister. What we are saying in effect is that we think the controls can be got rid of a great deal faster than they are being. But the government is asking for war-time controls and a further extension of them. If controls are inherently bad, there should be mo objection when we criticize this bill. The government should have gone farther; they should have thrown out the old bill and brought in a new bill so that we would not have been presented with this sort of strip-tease bill, half undressed and half clothed and then when we are just going to grasp it, it is suddenly fully clothed in its old garments-it is the old bill.
One further point before I come to the actual subject-matter of the principle of this bill. The Minister of Agriculture read the

preamble of the new bill, so that I assume I shall be forgiven if I deal briefly with that preamble. He said that it was very certain and very specific. I will not argue that point; I will accept his words on it. Referring to the measures taken under the War Measures Act, the preamble says:
And whereas in the existing circumstances it is essential that certain acts and things done and authorized and certain orders and regulations made under the War Measures Act be continued in force . . .
That is the preamble. We are told that it is only those acts and measures which are necessary for limited control that will be continued over the transitional period, but when we come to section 4 of the new bill t we find:
The orders and regulations made under the War Measures Act or pursuant to authority created under the said act in force immediately before the day this act comes into force shall, while this act is in force, continue in full force and effect . . .
Everything that was done under the War Measures Act is being continued under the provisions of this bill. We find that this burlesque, this strip-tease show is resolving itself into a simple farce and illusion and we are back again dealing with the original bill 'No. 15.
